﴿Those are the verses of the Book; and that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most of the people do not believe.﴾ The discussion regarding ﴿Those are the verses of the Book﴾ is like the discussion regarding its counterpart at the opening of Surah Yunus.
What is indicated by (Those) is what was revealed of the Qur'an before this verse, about which it is reported that it is "verses," that is, signs of inimitability (dala'il i'jaz). For this reason it is referred to with the demonstrative of the feminine, in consideration of the feminine gender of the predicate.

His saying ﴿and that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ may be a conjunction (atf) upon the clause ﴿Those are the verses of the Book﴾, so that ﴿and that which has been sent down to you﴾ is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun (idhar fi maqam al-idmar). It was not sufficient to conjoin a predicate to the predicate of the demonstrative; rather, a complete clause was brought, beginning with the relative pronoun, to define that the verses of the Book are sent down from Allah, for once it has been established that they are verses, this necessarily entails that they are sent down from Allah, and were it not so, they would not be verses.

He reports about that which was sent down, that it is the truth, using the form of restriction (qasr), that is, it is the truth and not any other of the books. The restriction is relative (idafi) with respect to known books among them, such as the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar, which al-Nadr ibn al-Harith knew. The intent is thus a refutation of the polytheists who claimed it to be like the fables of the ancients. Or the restriction is real but claimed (haqiqi idda'i) for the sake of emphasis, in that other books are not taken into account, that is, it is the complete truth, because the other books did not attain the ultimate of Allah's purpose for mankind, since they were stages leading to the highest stage. Therefore no book came except that its practice was abrogated or it was specified for a particular nation: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19].

It may also be that it is a conjunction of a singular noun upon his saying (the Book), a singular, by way of conjoining the attribute to the noun, like what al-Farra' recited:

To the stalwart king and the son of the Hammam, and the lion of the battalion, in the thronging crowd.

The use of (your Lord) rather than the name of majesty (ism al-jalala) is for gentleness (li al-talattuf). The "but" with his saying ﴿but most of the people do not believe﴾ refers to what the restriction conveyed of nullifying the equality of others with it in truth, a nullification that requires the removal of dispute over its being the most true; that is, but most of the people do not believe in what the proofs have indicated belief in. Because of this blameworthy disposition among them, the dispute among them over its being true continues.
The opening of the surah with this is an exhortation (tanwih) to what is in the Qur'an, of which this surah is a part, intended to prepare the listener to reflect on what will come to him of discourse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 2:

﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see. Then He istawa (established Himself) upon the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term.﴾ This is an initial resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i), the beginning of the main theme of the surah, and what precedes it serves as the preamble (dibaja) to a sermon. For this reason you will find that discourse on this theme has become lengthy and continuous.

The connection of this resumption to His saying ﴿But most people do not believe﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1] is that the root of their disbelief in the Qur'an arises from their clinging to disbelief and their habituation to arrogance and turning away from the call to the truth.

صفحة ٨٠
The opening with the Name of Majesty (Allah), rather than with a pronoun referring back to (your Lord), is because it is specific to Him, so that no other of their deities could be confused with Him, so that the intended statement applies to a specific referent that admits of no other, for the sake of emphatic conveyance in cutting off any trace of association (shirk).
"Alladhi rafa'a" (He who raised) is the predicate. It is made a relative construction (ism mawsul) because the relative clause is clearly understood to indicate that whoever is characterized by it is the one uniquely possessing lordship, since no one other than the One can accomplish such an act, and because this is accepted by them as well: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ The "heavens" (al-samawat) has been mentioned repeatedly; they are the wandering celestial bodies and the layers of the atmosphere in which they float.

"Raf'aha" (He raised them): He created them elevated, as one says, "Widen the collar of the robe and narrow its sleeve," not meaning "widen it after it was narrow" or "narrow it after it was wide," but rather "make it wide and make it narrow." Thus the meaning is not that He raised them after they had been low.

"Al-'amad" is the plural of 'imad (pillar), like ihab and uhub; the 'amid is that upon which the dome or house is raised. The clause (you see them) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the heavens, meaning there is no doubt that they are without pillars.

The discussion on the meaning of ﴿then He istawa upon the Throne﴾ has preceded in Surat al-A'raf and in Surat Yunus.

Likewise the discussion on "sakhkhara al-shams wal-qamar" (He subjected the sun and the moon) in His saying, ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], in Surat al-A'raf.

"Al-jary" (running): swift motion. The motion of the sun, moon, and stars across vast distances is the swiftest of movements of its kind, and that is their motion in their orbits.

صفحة ٨١
The "lam" is for causation (ta'lil). "Al-ajal" (term): it is the period which God has determined for the continuation of their motion, which is the duration of the solar system's order; if it becomes disordered, the worlds would be scattered and the Resurrection would occur.
"Al-musamma" (specified): its root meaning is that which is known by its name; here it is a metonymy for the specific and determined, since naming entails determination and distinction from confusion.

﴿He arranges the affair, and details the signs, that perhaps you may be certain of meeting your Lord.﴾ The clause (He arranges the affair) is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to the Name of Majesty. The clause "He details the signs" is a second circumstantial clause, left unconnected by conjunction to the preceding one, to make it in the style of enumeration and pausing, which indicates concern for its independence. The discussion of "yudabbir al-amr" was previously given at His saying ﴿And who arranges the affair﴾ [Yunus: 31] in Surat Yunus. The detailing of the signs was previously discussed at His saying ﴿Its verses were made firm, then detailed﴾ [Hud: 1] at the opening of Surat Hud.
The reason for combining the two here is that arranging the affair encompasses the determination of the first and second creation, so it points to the exercise of power through bringing into existence for intellects and worlds; and the detailing of the signs points to the exercise of power through establishing proofs and evidences. The effect of the two together is that people are guided to certainty that after this life there is another life, since reflecting with the intellect upon created things and their arrangement leads to that, and the detailing of the signs and proofs alerts the intellects and helps them and brings them closer to that guidance. This is close to His saying in Surat Yunus: ﴿He arranges the affair; there is no intercessor except after His permission. That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him. Will you not then remember?﴾ [Yunus: 3] ﴿To Him is your return, all together; the promise of Allah is true. Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it﴾ [Yunus: 4]. This is an incorporation (idmaj) of one purpose within another, since the discourse proceeds to establish divine oneness, and in the proofs of oneness there is also an indication of resurrection.

صفحة ٨٢
"Yudabbir" and "yufassil" are expressed in the present tense, contrary to His saying ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens﴾, because arranging and detailing are renewed and repeated with the renewal of the connection of power to what is empowered. As for raising the heavens and subjecting the sun and moon, these were completed and settled in a single instance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 3:

﴿It is He who spread out the earth and placed in it firm mountains and rivers, and of every kind of fruit He placed in it two mates, two.﴾ This is a conjunction (*'atf*, coordination) with the clause ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:2). Between the two clauses there is a kind of contrast: the first deals with the higher realms and their conditions, and the second with the lower realms. The meaning is that He is the Creator of all the realms and their accidents.

*Al-madd* means spreading out and extension, as in *zill madid* (an extended shade). From it comes *madd al-bahr* (the tide's rising), and *madda yadahu* (he extended his hand) when he spread it out. The meaning is that He created the earth spread out and wide, suitable for travel and sowing, because if He had made it into humps of rock or towering mountains pressed closely together, the living beings upon it could not easily benefit from it or travel from one place to another in search of sustenance and other needs. It is not intended that it was not spread out and that He then spread it; rather it is like His saying ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:2). This creation is therefore a sign pointing to power and to His gentleness toward His servants, and so it is both a sign and a favour.

*Al-rawasi* is the plural of *rasin*, which means firm and steadfast. The sense is mountains that are *rawasi*, and the noun it qualifies has been omitted because it is clear. This is like His saying ﴿And His are the ships running (*al-jawari*)﴾ (al-Rahman 55:24), meaning the ships that run. It will come later in His saying ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains (*rawasi*)﴾ (al-Nahl 16:15) in surah al-Nahl, in more detail than here.

The plural of *rasin* is given the pattern *fawa'il*, because the thing described is non-rational, and the pattern *fawa'il* is regular for plurals of adjectives applied to non-rational things, such as *sahil* and *bazil*.

Using the creation of mountains as evidence of great power is because their greatness is visible to the eye, unlike the creation of minerals and soil, which is hidden. As He, exalted is He, said ﴿And at the mountains, how they were set up?﴾ (al-Ghashiyah 88:19).

*Al-anhar* is the plural of *nahr*, which means a great valley. It was mentioned earlier in surah al-Baqarah in His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah will test you with a river﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:249). His saying ﴿and of every kind of fruit﴾ is a conjunction with *anharan*, so it is an object governed by *ja'ala fiha rawasiya* (He placed in it firm mountains). The insertion of *min* before *kull* follows Arabic usage when naming the kinds of non-rational things, as in His saying ﴿and He spread throughout it of every creature (*min kulli dabbah*)﴾ (al-Shura 42:29). This *min* is understood as partitive (*tab'id*), because the true natures of the kinds are not confined, and what exists of them is only some of the particular instances of the quiddity, since some of its instances have passed away and others will yet be brought into being.

What is meant by *al-thamarat* (the fruits) is the fruits themselves together with their trees. The fruits were mentioned because they are a locus of favour together with a lesson, as in His saying ﴿so We brought forth by it of every kind of fruit﴾ (al-A'raf 7:57). Therefore it is proper to pause at ﴿and of every kind of fruit﴾, and with that the enumeration of the created things connected to the earth is complete. This is the better explanation, and it is supported by a parallel in His saying ﴿He causes to grow for you by it crops, olives, date palms, grapes, and of every kind of fruit. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾ (al-Nahl 16:11) in surah al-Nahl.

It has been said that His saying ﴿and of every kind of fruit﴾ begins a new statement.

The phrase ﴿and of every kind of fruit﴾ is connected to ﴿He placed in it two mates, two﴾, and most exegetes explained it this way. But this is weakened, because on that reading there is no rhetorical point in fronting the prepositional phrase before its governing verb, since everything mentioned is a locus of concern, so there is no special emphasis here on fruits. Also, fruits do not admit of mates (*azwaj*), nor of there being two mates of two. Furthermore, this reading loses the favour of the creation of animals and their reproduction, although most of their benefit and livelihood comes from them. What brings this closer is His saying, on this same theme, ﴿Did We not make the earth a cradle, and the mountains as pegs, and create you in pairs?﴾ (al-Naba' 78:6-8). It is well known that the two mates (*zawjayn*) are the male and the female, as He said ﴿so He made of him the two mates, the male and the female﴾ (al-Qiyamah 75:39).

It is apparent that the clause ﴿He placed in it two mates﴾ is a resumptive new statement (*mustanfa'ah*), for the sake of attention to this kind of created thing, namely the kind of animals, created in two categories, male and female, each one of which is a mate (*zawj*) with the other. The application of *zawj* to the male and the female of animals is common, as mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell you and your mate (*zawjuka*) in the Garden﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:35) in surah al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿and from it created its mate (*zawjaha*)﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:1) at the beginning of surah al-Nisa', and His saying ﴿We said: carry in it of every pair, two (*min kulli zawjayni ithnayn*)﴾ (Hud 11:40). As for His saying ﴿and We caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair (*zawj bahij*)﴾ (Qaf 50:7), this is an application of *zawj* to a category, on the basis of the commonness of its application to the male category and the female category. It was used figuratively for any category at all, not characterised by male or female, by way of the relation of generality (*'alaqat al-itlaq*). The indication (*qarinah*) is His saying *anbatna* (We caused to grow), in the absence of the dual. Similarly is His saying ﴿and We brought forth by it mates (*azwaj*) of diverse plants﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:53) in surah Ta-Ha.

The indefiniteness of *zawjayn* is for classification (*tanwi'*), that is, He placed two mates of every kind. The dual sense in *zawjayn* is that each single member of the pair is itself called a *zawj*, as mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿eight mates: of the sheep two, and of the goats two﴾ (al-An'am 6:143) and what follows, in surah al-An'am.

The description with the words *ithnayn* (two, two) is for emphasis, in order to confirm the favour.

﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ (*yughshi al-layla al-nahar*). Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.

The clause *yughshi* (He covers) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *ja'ala* (He placed). The present tense was used for it because of the renewal that it implies, since the placing of the things previously mentioned is a fixed and continuous placing, whereas the covering of night and day is a matter renewed every day and night. This is an inference drawn from the accidents of the conditions of the earth. Its mention alongside the signs of the lower realm is of the utmost scientific precision, because night and day are accidents of the terrestrial sphere according to its orientation towards the sun, and they are not conditions of the heavens, since the sun and the stars do not change their state by light and darkness.

The discussion of the parallel to His saying ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ (al-A'raf 7:54) has already been given at the beginning of surah al-A'raf.

The majority read *yughshi* with a sunken *ghayn* and a light *shin*, present tense of *aghsha*. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read it with a doubled *shin*, present tense of *ghashsha*.

His saying *inna fi dhalika la-ayat* (indeed in that are signs) refers to what was mentioned earlier from His saying ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:2) up to here, by interpreting the things mentioned as one thing.

The things mentioned were made into containers (*zuruf*) for *ayat* (signs), because each one of the matters mentioned contains great signs which clear reasoning and reflection free of illusions makes manifest. For this reason the attribute of reflection was applied to the word *qawm* (people), indicating that repeated and renewed reflection is an established trait in them, to the point that it was made one of the constituents of their national character, that is, their natural disposition. This has been explained in our discussion of the indication of the word *qawm* on this point at His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason (*ya'qilun*)﴾ in surah al-Baqarah.

In this there is a hint that those who attributed reflection to themselves among the naturalists, who explained the origin of existing things from matter and denied the choosing agent, did not reflect except with a deficient reflection mixed with illusions, which is not what the nature of reason requires, since causes and derivative effects were confused for them with the origin of creation and bringing into being.

For reflection (*tafakkur*) the form that indicates effort (*takalluf*) was used, and the present tense, to indicate intense and repeated reflection.

Reflection (*tafakkur*) was discussed at His saying ﴿Will you not reflect?﴾ in surah al-An'am.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 4:

﴿And on the earth are adjoining tracts, and gardens of grapevines, and crops, and palm trees, some clustered and some not clustered, watered with one water; yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason.﴾

For Allah is the eloquence of the Qur'an in changing the style upon moving to mention the blessings that indicate the power of Allah the Exalted in what He inspired people with of working the land, by ploughing it, sowing it, planting it,

Page 86

and tending to it. So that is joined (ma'tufan) to the things whose making Allah the Exalted attributed, but it is not attributed to Allah until He reaches His saying ﴿and We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾, because that is due to secrets which Allah the Exalted deposited within them, which are the cause of their differing. And such lessons and drawing of attention are among what the Qur'an has uniquely possessed among all the books.

The apparent noun "the earth" is repeated instead of its pronoun, which would be the expected form, so that the sentence stands independently and the style is renewed. The original arrangement of the sentence would have been: "He placed in it two spouses, and in it adjoining tracts," but he turned to this for clarification and brevity.

Qita' (al-qita'): the plural of qit'ah with a kasra on the qaf, which is a part of a thing, likened to what is cut off. The describing of the tracts as "adjoining" (mutajawirat) is not intended in itself in this context, since it is not the locus of the lesson of the signs; rather, the intended meaning is a deleted description indicated by the context, whose estimate is: "differing in colours and growths," as indicated by His saying ﴿and We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾.

It was described as "adjoining" because differing in colours and growths together with adjacency is more indicative of great power. This is like His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of differing colours, and jet-black﴾ [Fatir: 27].

So the meaning of ﴿adjoining tracts﴾ is: plots that differ while being adjacent and contiguous. Restricting the mention to the earth and its tracts points to a difference arising in it not from human making, namely the difference of pastures and herbage. The mere mention of the tracts suffices for that, so he refers them to the well-known observation of the difference in the growths of tracts of land in pasture and herbage, which are the grazing grounds of their livestock and beasts. For this reason no mention is made here of the difference in their food, since there is no taste for humans in it, but it differs in what some animals eat compared with others.

The discussion of ﴿and gardens of grapevines﴾ has already been covered at His saying ﴿and from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapevines﴾ [al-An'am: 99].

Page 87

Crops (zar') have been covered at His saying ﴿and the palm and the crops, differing in their produce﴾ [al-An'am: 141]. Nakhil (palm trees) is the collective noun of a palm tree in the same way as nakhl; it has been covered in that verse, and both occur in Surah al-An'am.

Crops are found in the gardens, sown between their trees. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-zar'in wa-nakhilin" in the genitive, in coordination with a'nab; Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs and Ya'qub read them in the nominative in coordination with "jannat". The meaning is one, because the crops that are in the gardens are equal to those outside them, so the mention of one suffices, in fulfilment of the requirement of brevity. Likewise, on the reading of the nominative, it dispenses with mention of the crops that are in the gardens, and the palm tree is only found in gardens.

Sinwan: the plural of sinw with a kasra on the sad in the most eloquent usage for both, which is the dialect of the Hijaz, and with a damma on it too, which is the dialect of Tamim and Qays. The sinw is a palm tree gathered together with another palm tree, both growing from a single root, or a group of palm trees. The singular is sinw, the dual sinwan without tanwin, and the plural sinwan with tanwin, a broken plural. This pattern is rare among the dual forms, and of the plurals in Arabic only five have been preserved: sinw and sinwan; qinw and qinwan; zid, meaning "like", and zidan; shiqdh, with a dhal dotted, the name of the chameleon, and shiqdhan; and hishsh, meaning garden, and hishshan.

The palm tree was singled out for mention of the attribute "sinwan" because the lesson in it is stronger. The purpose of adding "wa-ghayru sinwan" (and not sinwan) is to renew the lesson through the difference of states.

The majority read "sinwani wa-ghayri sinwani" with the genitive on "sinwan" and the genitive on "ghayr", in coordination with "zar'" (in the genitive); Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs and Ya'qub read both in the nominative in coordination with "wa-jannat".

Al-saqy: giving a drink to be drunk. What is meant by "water" here is rain water and river water, and it is one with respect to what is watered, by some of it.

Page 88

Al-tafdil (preference): a favour bestowed by the more excellent, a lesson in it and in its opposite, and a metonymy for difference.

The majority read "tuqa" with a feminine prefix, in consideration of the plural "jannat"; Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub read "yuqa" with a masculine prefix, on the interpretation of what has been mentioned.

The majority read "wa-nufaddilu" with the first person plural of majesty; Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "wa-yufaddilu" with a masculine prefix, and the pronoun refers to the Name of Majesty in His saying ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. The feminine form of "ba'dhaha" is used by those who read "yuqa" with a masculine prefix, rather than saying "ba'dhahu", because what is intended is that He makes some of the gardens excel others in fruit.

Al-akl (the food): with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf, and it is that which is eaten. It is permissible in the language to put a damma on the kaf.

The adverbial sense of "in the food" (zarfiyyat al-tafdil fi al-ukl) is an adverbial in the sense of association, because the excellence appears in what is eaten; that is, We make some gardens excel others, or some grapevines, crops and palm trees excel others of their kind by what they bring forth. The meaning is that the difference of their flavours and their excellence, while the root is one and the nourishment by water is one, is nothing but hidden powers which Allah deposited in them, so their effects came out differing.

From this came the sentence ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ coming as a concluding clause (tadhyil).

The demonstrative "that" (dhalika) refers to the whole of what has been mentioned from His saying ﴿And He is the One who spread out the earth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3], and the whole of what has been mentioned has been placed in the position of an adverb for the signs. Its indication of His being singled out for divinity has been made into many indications, since in each of them there is a sign indicating that.

The signs have been described as belonging to "those who reason", as an allusion that those whom those signs do not convince are placed in the position of those who do not reason. And the indication that reason is an innate disposition of those who benefited from those signs has been increased by applying the attribute of reason to the word "qawm" (people), as an indication that reason is among the constituents of their peoplehood, as we explained in the verse before it.

﴿But if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" They are those who disbelieve in their Lord. They are those with shackles around their necks. They are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾

This is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the sentence ﴿Allah is the One who raised the heavens without visible pillars﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. When the argument for divine Oneness (tawhid) had been fully established, the discourse shifted to refuting those who denied resurrection (al-ba'th). This is an independent and intended theme of this surah. It had been introduced earlier, during the argument for Oneness, through the words ﴿so that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2] as a preparation for what is here. The discourse then moved to it independently, occasioned by demonstrating the greatness of God's power, drawing on the proofs mentioned earlier, as in His words ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation? Nay, they are in confusion about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15], and His words ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾ [al-Tariq: 8]. It was phrased in the form of amazement at the denial of those who deny resurrection, because the previous proofs left them no excuse in that matter, so their denial became a matter for the amazement of one who wonders.

The purpose of the conditional here is not, as is usual with conditionals, to make the occurrence of the consequent depend on the occurrence of the protasis. The saying "When we are dust, shall we...?" is an amazing thing whether or not anyone is amazed by it. Rather, the intended meaning is that if there is any state of amazement, then their saying is the most deserving of every amazement from every one who wonders. Accordingly, the address may be directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), which suits what follows it: ﴿and they urge you to hasten the evil before the good﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6], and what follows that of address that is suitable only to the Prophet (ﷺ). It may also be that the address here is to an unspecified person, like ﴿If only you could see when the criminals hang their heads﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12].

The verb occurring in the context of a conditional is not intended to be linked to a specific object. So one does not supply "If you are amazed at a saying" or "If you are amazed at a denial." Rather, the verb is treated as intransitive and no object is supplied for it. The sense is: if there is amazement in you, then be amazed at their saying, etc.

Moreover, the occurrence of the verb in a conditional context resembles its occurrence in a negative context, so it carries general scope over its objects in the rhetorical setting. That is: if you are amazed at anything, then their saying is amazing. It may also be that the clause ﴿And if you are amazed﴾ etc. is a conjunction on the clause ﴿But most people do not believe﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1]. The sense would then be: if you are amazed at their not believing that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, then their denial of resurrection is amazing.

The purpose of this is to create suspense, so that the one being wondered at is recognized, magnifying it or something similar. For this reason the indefiniteness in His words ﴿then amazing﴾ indicates variety, because the intended meaning is that their saying is fit to be an object of amazement. Moreover, it conveys the sense of glorification in its own domain, following what the conditional phrasing conveyed of suspense.

The interrogative in ﴿When we are dust...﴾ is a denial (inkari), because they are certain that they will not be in a new creation after becoming dust. The saying reported of them has the meaning of a question about two matters together: their becoming dust, and the renewal of their creation a second time. The intended meaning is amazement and the claim that it is impossible (al-ihalah).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿a-idhā kunnā turāban﴾ with an interrogative hamza at its beginning before the hamza of (idhā). Ibn ʿAmir read it without the interrogative hamza.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿a-innā la-fī khalqin jadīd﴾ with an interrogative hamza before the hamza of (innā). Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Ja'far read it without the interrogative hamza.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿They are those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾ serves to draw attention to the fact that they deserve what comes after the demonstrative as a predicate, because of what preceded the demonstrative, namely their saying ﴿When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, after they had seen the proofs of the first creation. Thus, by their saying that, two rulings are established against them. One is that they disbelieved in their Lord, because whoever says ﴿When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ is none but a disbeliever in Allah, that is, in the attributes of the divine state (bi-sifat al-hay'ah), since they made Him unable to restore His creation. The second is that they deserve punishment.

[Page 90]

The sentence ﴿And they are those with shackles around their necks﴾ is conjoined to this sentence. It is introduced by the demonstrative for the same purpose for which the preceding sentence was introduced. The content of the two preceding sentences establishes that they deserve to have shackles placed around their necks, and that is the recompense of humiliation. Similarly, the sentence ﴿And they are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾ is conjoined.

His words ﴿shackles around their necks﴾ are a threat of driving them to the reckoning in the manner of humiliation and subjugation. They used to place shackles on captives who were heavily bound. Al-Nabighah said:

Or a free woman like a desert gazelle, whose wrists and hamstrings were bound with bracelets of iron,

She calls out to Qu'ayn while the iron has bitten her, biting like a sword-belt upon hollow reeds.

Al-aghlal (shackles) is the plural of ghull (with a dammah on the ghayn), which is the chain placed on the neck, and it is the strongest form of restraint. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When the shackles are around their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. The repetition of the demonstrative three times is for magnification.

The sentence ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾ explains the sentence "companions of the Fire."

[Page 92]

The clause (﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾) is coordinated with the clause (﴿And if you wonder [at their denial], then wondrous is their saying﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5]), because both clauses relate their strange conduct in obstinacy, stubbornness, and mocking the threat. He began by mentioning their denial of the threat of the Hereafter, because they denied the Resurrection, and then he coordinated with it their denial of the threat of this world, because they denied the Messenger (ﷺ). In their mockery of the threat of the descent of punishment, and in their considering it impossible, they were in a state where they had witnessed the traces of the punishment that had descended upon the nations before them. This was only due to their distraction from the power of God, Exalted, which preceded the speech as evidence for it and as a basis derived from it. So they hasten its descent upon them in contempt and ridicule, like their saying ﴿Rain down upon us stones from the heaven, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and their saying ﴿Or you cause the heaven to fall upon us in fragments, as you claim﴾ [al-Isra': 92].

The "bi" in (with the evil) serves to make the verb transitive to what it did not previously take as an object. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿What you seek to hasten is not with me﴾ [al-An'am: 57], in Surat al-An'am.

The "sayyi'a" (evil) is the bad state, and here it is the calamity that afflicts whoever it befalls. The "hasana" (good) is its opposite; that is, they asked for signs that contain punishment with evil, like their saying ﴿If this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the heaven﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], without asking for a sign of goodness.

This verse was revealed as a narration of some of their questions, which they considered to be a challenge, and by which they indicated mockery of the punishment.

The priority of the evil is a conventional priority (qabliyya i'tibariyya), that is, they choose the evil over the good. Its verification will come at His saying ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you hasten the evil before the good?"﴾ [al-Naml: 46], in Surat al-Naml, so refer to it there.

The clause (﴿And the exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). It is the place of increased wonder, because they might have an excuse if they had not seen the traces of the punished nations, such as 'Ad and Thamud.

"Al-mathulat" (with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the tha') is the plural of "mathula" (with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the tha', like "samura"), and with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the tha' (like "'urfa"): it is the severe punishment which becomes an example by which punishments are exemplified.

The clause ﴿And your Lord is certainly Full of forgiveness for the people despite their wrongdoing﴾ is coordinated with the clause (﴿And the exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾). This is an exposure of their delusion through the delay of the punishment from them, because when they mocked the Prophet (ﷺ) and sought the arrival of punishment upon them, and saw that its arrival was not hastened for them, they were seized by a violent persistence in denial, and they reckoned the delay of the punishment to be the weakness of the one who threatens. They denied the Prophet (ﷺ) while ignorant that God is Forbearing, granting respite to His servants, perhaps they will return. So forgiveness here is used in the sense of temporary forgiveness, which is overlooking the violence of their denial and delaying the punishment until a term, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a specified community, they will surely say, "What is holding it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and what they used to mock will encompass them﴾ [Hud: 8].

The evidence for this is that the discourse concerns the punishment of this world, which admits of delay, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little, but you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15], meaning the punishment of this world, which is the hunger with which Quraysh was afflicted after it had been feeding them from hunger. The "ʿalā" in His saying (despite their wrongdoing) means "maʿa" (with).

The context of the verse indicates that the intended forgiveness here is overlooking the polytheists in this world by delaying their punishment until a term God willed, or until the Day of Reckoning. The punishment mentioned in His saying ﴿And your Lord is certainly severe in punishment﴾ is the opposite of that forgiveness, namely the punishment deferred in this world or the punishment of the Day of Reckoning. Therefore, the meaning of wrongdoing (zulm) is taken according to what is well known in the terminology of the Qur'an, where it is applied to polytheism (shirk).

It is also permissible to take wrongdoing as the committing of sins, by the evidence of the context, as in its use in His saying ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things that had been lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 160]. There is then no contradiction at all between this interpretation and His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], as is evident.

The benefit of this addition is to show the intensity of God's mercy toward His servants in this world, as He said: ﴿And if Allah were to seize the people for what they earned, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a creature, but He defers them to a specified term﴾ [Fatir: 45].

The clause ﴿And your Lord is certainly severe in punishment﴾ is a precaution (ihtiras) lest they suppose that the forgiveness mentioned is a permanent forgiveness, implying allusively that punishment will befall them afterward.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 7:

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.﴾ It is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause (﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6]) and what follows. This is a state of their strange conduct, namely that they do not take into account the signs with which Muhammad ﷺ was supported, the greatest of which is the verses of the Qur'an. So they continue to ask for a sign as they propose it, and thus it is connected to the clause (﴿But most people do not believe﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1]).

What they mean by "sign" here is a supernatural occurrence according to what they propose. It differs from what came earlier in His saying "they ask you to hasten the evil before the good," because that was about hastening what He threatened them with. What is here concerns the coming of a sign that confirms him, like their saying ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8].

Because their proposing a sign reveals their deeming its occurrence impossible, owing to their ignorance of the great power of God Most High, this is placed among the consequences of His great power, as indicated by the saying of God Most High in Surat al-An'am: ﴿They say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed God is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."﴾ [al-An'am: 37].

By this, the linking of the clauses to one another and the branching of all of them from the principal purpose is organized. Those who disbelieve are the very same as the referent of the pronoun in (﴿they ask you to hasten﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 54]), and he turned away from their pronoun to the relative noun to add emphasis to recording disbelief upon them, and because of what the relative pronoun implies as a justification for the issuing of their saying.

Page 95
The form of the present tense indicates the recurrence and repetition of that. "Lawla" (لولا) is a particle of urging (tahdid). By urging they feign that they are eager and desirous for a sign other than the Qur'an to be sent down so that they may believe, and they are lying in that, since if they were given a sign as they propose they would disbelieve in it, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We did not refrain from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾ [al-Isra': 59].

God has rejected their proposal at its root by His saying ﴿You are only a warner﴾, restricting the Prophet ﷺ to the attribute of warning; this is a restriction relative to a specific circumstance (qasr idafi), meaning: you are a warner, not a producer of supernatural occurrences. By this the reason for restricting him to warning rather than good tidings becomes clear, because it is a relative restriction with respect to his circumstances with the polytheists.

The clause ﴿and for every people there is a guide﴾ is a concluding generalization (tadhyil bi-al-a'amm). That is: you are only a warner to these people for their guidance; and for every people there is a guide whom God sent to warn them, so that perhaps they may be guided. So you were not a novelty among the messengers, and it was not for messengers before you to have signs according to the proposals of their peoples; rather their signs were according to what God willed to manifest through their hands. Moreover, the miracles of the messengers come according to what suits the condition of those to whom they were sent.

Since those among whom the call of Muhammad ﷺ appeared were Arabs, people of eloquence and rhetoric, God made his greatest miracle the Qur'an, in a clear Arabic tongue. To this meaning the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the authentic hadith refers: "There is no prophet except that he was given of the signs what людей believed upon because of it, but what I was given is a revelation which God revealed to me, so I hope that I will have the most followers on the Day of Resurrection."

By this generality obtained through the concluding clause, which includes the Messenger ﷺ, the meaning becomes: you are only a warner to your people, a guide leading them to the truth. For warning and guidance are mutually entailing: there is no warning except that it is guidance, and no guidance except that it contains warning, and guidance is more general than warning. In this there is a wonderful interlacing (ihtibak).

Page 96
The majority (al-Jumhur) read "hadin" (هادٍ) without a ya' at its end, both in pause and in continuation. In continuation, this is because of the meeting of two quiescent letters: the quiescence of the ya' and the quiescence of the tanwin, which must be pronounced in continuation. In pause it follows the continuation state. It is an eloquent dialect and it follows the orthography of the Mushaf. Ibn Kathir read it in continuation like the majority. He read it with the ya' affirmed in pause, since the cause for deleting the ya' has ceased; this is a sound dialect.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verses 8–9:**

﴿Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs diminish and what they increase. And everything with Him is in measure.﴾ ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted.﴾

This is a transition to the argument for God's exclusive divinity (al-infirad bi-l-ilahiyya), and it is connected to the sentence ﴿Allah is the One who raised the heavens﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2] and what follows.

This sentence is a new independent statement (isti'naf ibtida'i, a resumptive sentence beginning a fresh topic). When the many proofs in the preceding verses had established God's oneness in creation and management, and His great power by which He placed subtle details of creation in His creatures, the discourse moved to affirming that He has knowledge: a general knowledge of the subtle and the great things alike. For this reason it opens in the same manner as the previous topic, beginning with the name of majesty (ism al-jalala), just as the previous topic began with it in His saying ﴿Allah is the One who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2].

This sentence was placed here because it is related to their saying ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. What was mentioned in it of God's knowledge and His great craftsmanship is suitable to be a proof that He is not unable to bring what they demanded of signs. However, the purpose of sending the Messenger is not disputation, but rather a call to reflect on the evidences.

[p. 97]

Since God's creation of the worlds and other things was known to the polytheists, but their devotion to idol-worship distracts them from remembering it, they did not need more than reminder of it and alerting them to what might be hidden of the subtle details of creation, such as His saying just before (without pillars) and His saying ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], and so on. The report about creation in the verse ﴿Allah is the One who raised the heavens﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2] and so on was phrased in the manner of the relative construction (al-mawsul), to indicate knowledge of the established content of the relative clause concerning the subject of the report.

In that relative clause the past tense was used, ﴿raised﴾, as we pointed out just before. Here, however, the report is phrased in the present tense, which indicates renewal and recurrence, to convey that this knowledge is continual and newly connected according to the conditions of the various and numerous things known, in the manner established in His saying ﴿He manages the affair, detailing the signs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2].

Mention was made of some of God's knowledge about which no one among creatures on that day disputes, and their deities are not consulted about it. This is by way of example, establishing the particular in order to establish the universal. So ﴿what every female carries﴾ refers to the embryos of humans and animals. For this reason the verb "carries" (hamala) was used rather than "is pregnant" (habala), because habal is specific to a woman's pregnancy.

And ﴿ma﴾ is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and its generality requires God's knowledge of the state of the existing pregnancy, whether male or female, complete or deficient, beautiful or ugly, long or short, and of its colour.

And ﴿taghid﴾ means "diminishes." The apparent meaning is that it is a metonymy (kinaya) for conception, because the diminishing of the womb is the stopping of menstrual blood from it, and its increasing is the flowing of menstruation from it. It is also permissible that "diminishing" is a metaphor (isti'ara) for the absence of multiplicity.

And "increasing" (izdiyad) means multiplicity, that is, what is in the wombs of one embryo or of several embryos; this applies to humans and animals.

The clause ﴿and everything with Him is in measure﴾ is coordinated (ma'tufa) with the clause ﴿knows what every female carries﴾. So what is meant by "thing" is a thing among the known things. The phrase ﴿with Him﴾ may be a predicate of ﴿everything﴾, and ﴿in measure﴾ may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to ﴿everything﴾. It is also permissible that ﴿with Him﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause relative to ﴿measure﴾, and ﴿in measure﴾ is the predicate of ﴿everything﴾.

[p. 98]

"Miqdar" (measure) is a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi), as indicated by the preposition "bi-", meaning "by determination." Its meaning is specification and precise control. The meaning is that He knows everything with detailed knowledge, without vagueness or ambiguity. In this there is a refutation of the non-Muslim philosophers who said that the Necessary Existent knows universals but does not know particulars, fleeing from the attachment of knowledge to events. The scholars of kalam (theological discourse) refuted their doctrine with what leaves nothing beyond it. This is a universal proposition establishing the generality of His knowledge, after the generality had been established by way of example through His knowledge of the hidden particulars in His saying ﴿Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾.

The clause ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) and a summation (fadhlaka) to generalize the knowledge to the hidden and the apparent, which are the two divisions of existing things. The mention of the unseen was already made at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara.

As for "the witnessed" (al-shahada), here it is a verbal noun with the meaning of the passive participle, that is, "the things witnessed," which are the apparent and sensed things: visible things and other sensed things. So the purpose of "the unseen and the witnessed" is to generalize existing things, like His saying ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ [al-Haqqa: 38] ﴿and what you do not see﴾ [al-Haqqa: 39].

"Al-Kabir" (the Great) is a metaphor for greatness, since the use of names of quantity and words of size for greatness has become common, by likening the intelligible to the sensible, and this became so widespread that it became like a literal meaning. "Al-Muta'ali" means the one who is exalted. The attribute was formed in the pattern of reciprocal form (tafa'ul) to indicate that loftiness is an essential attribute of Him, not from another, that is, the One who is raised to a rank that is rationally necessary for Him. The meaning of "raising" here is a metaphor for complete might, such that no existing thing can overcome or compel Him, or it means the one exempt from deficiencies, as in His, mighty and majestic, saying ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate﴾ [al-Nahl: 3].

The deletion of the "ya'" from "al-Muta'ali" is for the sake of the verse-endings (fawasil), which end in unvoweled consonants. This is because the preferred form for a defective noun (manqus) that is not nunated is to retain the "ya'" in pause, except when it falls in the rhyme (qafiya) or in the verse-endings, as in this verse, to match ﴿min walin﴾ and ﴿al-asal﴾.

Sibawayh mentioned that what is preferred to retain of the "ya'" and "waw" sounds is deleted in verse-endings and rhymes. Retention is more analogous (aqyas), and deletion is common in Arabic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 10:

﴿It is the same whether one of you conceals his speech or speaks openly, and whether he hides by night or goes forth freely by day.﴾ The position of this sentence is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because its content stands in the position of a conclusion drawn from the all-encompassing knowledge of God Most High regarding the hidden and the manifest. He turned away from the third-person pronouns used in what preceded to direct address here, in His words (﴿سَواءٌ مِنكُمْ﴾), because it is an instruction suitable for both believers and disbelievers.

Within it there is also an implicit threat (ta'rid bil-tahdid) directed at the polytheists who plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ).

"Sawa'" (سَواءٌ) is a noun meaning "equal" (mustawin). Its meaning normally falls between two things or more. It is used in speech in a fixed form, so one says: "they two are sawa'" and "they are sawa'," and God Most High said: ﴿So you are equal in it﴾ [al-Rum: 28]. The position of "sawa'" here is that of the subject (mubtada'). And "﴿man asarra al-qawl﴾" ("whoever conceals speech") is an agent (fa'il) that took the place of the predicate (khabar). It is permissible to make "sawa'" the fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), with "man asarra" as the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and "minkum" ("of you") as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from "asarra."

Al-istikhfa' (الِاسْتِخْفاء) here means concealment (al-khafa'). The sin and the ta' are for intensification of the verb, like istajaba.

Al-sarib (السّارِبُ) is an active participle from sariba, meaning he went along the sarb, with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the ra', which means the path. This is one of the verbs derived from fixed nouns (al-af'al al-mushtaqqa min al-asma' al-jamida). The mention of concealment with the night is because it is more hidden, and the mention of going forth with the day is because it is more apparent. The meaning is that these two categories are equal in the knowledge of God Most High.

The waw that conjoins the relative nouns to the first relative is for division (lil-taqsim), so it carries the meaning of "or" (bi-ma'na aw).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 11:

﴿For him there are successive angels before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of Allah.﴾ The sentence "for him there are successive angels" (lahu mu'aqqibat) to its end may be connected to the relative pronoun (man) in His words ﴿whether one of you conceals speech or speaks openly therewith, and whether one hides by night or goes forth in daylight﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10]. In that case the sentence is a second predicate of "whoever conceals speech" and what is conjoined to it.

Its derivation is from al-'aqib (with a fatha then a kasra), which is the noun for the rear of the foot; so it is a verb derived from a fixed noun, because the one who follows another is as if he treads on his heel. The "hifz" (guarding) is observation (muraqaba), and from it the Watcher (al-raqib) is named Hafiz. The meaning is: they observe each person in his states, whether in secrecy or in openness, in stillness or in motion; that is, in the states of those things. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10].

This is a parenthetical sentence placed between the preceding sentences, which are brought as evidence for the great power of Allah and His knowledge of His creation, and between the reminder of the strength of His power, and the sentence ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12]. The purpose is to warn them against persisting in polytheism by warning them of the arrival of punishment in this world, in contrast to their hastening for evil before good. That is because they were in a state of ease of life, so they became insolent with the blessing, met the call of the Messenger ﷺ with mockery, and treated the believers with contempt. They said ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], and ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, the people of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

Allah reminded them of His blessing upon them and alerted them that its removal would not occur except because of their evil deeds, after they had been warned and called.

"Taghyir" is substitution by a contrary. Therefore it is clearly a threat to the people of luxury among the polytheists, that they have exposed themselves to its change. So "ma" in "what" (ma) as a relative is a condition, and the "ba'" is for accompaniment, meaning a condition accompanying a people, that is, a condition of blessing, because it is the place of warning against change; as for other conditions, their change is desired. The word "change" in His words "until they change" is used for causing it, in the manner of metonymy of the cause (al-majaz al-'aqli).

Since the context is one of fear and dread, it requires explicitness rather than allusion or anything near it. That is, when Allah intends to change what is with a people at the time they change what is in themselves, nothing turns back His will. This is a warning against delusion, that they say: "We will continue on what we are in; when we see the punishment, we will believe." This is like His words ﴿Why was there not a town that believed so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus﴾ [Yunus: 98], and so on.

The sentence ﴿and they have besides Him no patron﴾ is an addition to the warning against delusion, lest they think that their idols are their intercessors with Allah.

The "wali" is the one who takes charge of someone's affair, that is, occupies himself with his affair with management and benefit. It is derived from waliya, meaning he drew near, and it is nearness of association and treatment.

The majority read "min wal" with tanwin on "wal" without a yaʾ in pause and in continuation. Ibn Kathir read it with a yaʾ after the lam only in pause, not in continuation, as you have learned in His words ﴿And whomever Allah misguides, for him there is no guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33] in this surah.

﴿He it is who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and who produces the heavy clouds﴾ ﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and so do the angels, out of awe of Him. All of this suits the aims of the preceding verses, His saying ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8] and His saying ﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8]. Therefore this sentence deserves to stand independently and to be brought as a new sentence, so that it is self-standing among the independent sentences that come in the purpose of the sūrah.

It comes here in the form of direct address, in the style of His saying ﴿Whether among you is one who conceals speech﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10], because fear and hope proceed from the believers, and the disbelievers are threatened by them.

[p. 104]

He made the lightning a sign both of warning and of good tidings together, because they used to name the lightning and thereby anticipate the rain, and they used to fear its thunderbolts.

The "producing of the clouds" (inshā' al-saḥāb) means its formation from nothing, by stirring up the vapours which gather into clouds.

Al-saḥāb is a collective noun (ism jam') for saḥāba. Al-thiqāl is the plural of thaqīla. Heaviness (al-thiql) is a body's having a greater quantity of parts than its like. Heaviness is therefore a relative matter that varies with the differing kinds of bodies: something may be considered heavy in its kind while being light relative to another kind. A cloud is heavy to the extent of the vapour within it. The sign of its heaviness is its nearness to the earth and the slowness of its movement by the winds. The light one of them is called jahām.

He joined the thunder to the mention of the lightning and the clouds, because it accompanies them in many circumstances.

Since the thunder is a mighty sound, its mention was made a lesson for the listeners, because the thunder, through rational implications, points to the fact that Allah is exalted above what the polytheists say in claiming partners. And since the nature of that indication is to move the one who considers it to glorify Allah above having a partner, He made the sound of thunder a proof of Allah's exaltedness. The "bi-" in "with His praise" is for accompaniment (mulābasa), meaning: it glorifies Allah with a glorification accompanied by His praise, in that it indicates the approach of the descent of rain, which is a blessing that requires praise. The discussion of the thunder's accompaniment of praise is equivalent to the discussion of the attribution of glorification to the thunder. So the accompaniment is either a rational metaphor or an implicit metaphor.

And "the angels" (al-malā'ika) is conjoined to "the thunder," meaning: and the angels glorify [Allah] out of His awe, i.e., out of fear of Allah.

The "min" in "out of awe" is causal, meaning: they glorify Allah for the sake of fear of Him, i.e., fear of what He does not approve, which is falling short in glorifying Him.

[p. 105]

This is a parenthetical statement inserted between the enumeration of admonitions, for the sake of allusion to the polytheists: that is, the glorification which the signs of the atmosphere indicate is performed by the angels, so Allah is independent of your glorifying Him, as in His saying ﴿If you disbelieve, indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾ [al-Zumar: 7], and His saying ﴿Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on earth all together, indeed Allah is free of need and praiseworthy﴾ [Ibrahim: 8].

As for the thunder, it is an instrument of frightening and warning, as He said in the verse of Surat al-Baqara: ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, wherein is darkness, thunder, and lightning; they put their fingers in their ears against the thunderclaps, for fear of death﴾ [al-Baqara: 19]. Of this kind is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed the sun and the moon are two signs among the signs of Allah; Allah frightens His servants by them." That is, by their eclipse. Thus, in regard to their being signs, mention is restricted to warning, since people do not expect any benefit from their eclipse.

The sentence ﴿while they dispute about Allah﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because it is one of the completions of the astonishment in His saying ﴿And if you are astonished, then astonishing is their saying﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5], etc. Thus all the third-person pronouns refer to the disbelievers who were mentioned at the beginning of the sūrah in His saying ﴿But most people do not believe﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1], His saying ﴿Those are they who disbelieved in their Lord﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5], and His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. The style has been returned here to third-person pronouns, since the discourse concluded on what is suitable for admonishing both believers and disbelievers, so the warning became purely directed at the disbelievers.

Disputation (al-mujādala) is contention and argument by speech. It was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 107] in Surat al-Nisa'.

It has been understood that the object of "they dispute" (yujādilūna) is the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. So the estimate is: "they dispute with you" or "they dispute with you all," as in His saying ﴿They argue with you about the truth after it has become clear﴾ [al-Anfal: 6] in Surat al-Anfal.

[p. 106]

Disputation occurs only concerning affairs and conditions, so attaching the Divine Name in the genitive to the verb "they dispute" must necessarily be on the estimate of an omitted noun (muḍāf) indicated by the context, i.e., "concerning the Oneness of Allah" or "concerning His power to resurrect."

Among their disputation is what His saying related: ﴿Has not man seen that We created him from a drop, and then he is an open adversary?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 77] ﴿And he presents to Us a parable and forgets his creation; he says: Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78], in Surat Ya-Sin.

So it is answered with ﴿mighty in plotting﴾, in the manner of mushākala (matching of terms), i.e., He is mighty in stratagem; they cannot overcome Him. A parallel is His saying ﴿And they plotted, and Allah plotted, and Allah is the best of plotters﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54].

Niftawayh said: it is from māḥala ʿan amrihi, meaning "he argued." The meaning is: He is mighty in disputation, i.e., strong in argument.

If the mīm is augmentative, then it is a mif'al from al-ḥawl, meaning "strength." On this view, the conversion of the waw into an alif is irregular, since there is no reason for the change, because the letter before the waw is quiescent with a living quiescence. Perhaps they changed it to an alif to distinguish it from miḥwal, meaning a child with a ḥawl, i.e., a year old.

Al-Wahidi and al-Tabari mention reports from Anas and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that this verse was revealed concerning the case of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'a, when they came to Madina stipulating conditions for their entering Islam, which the Prophet (ﷺ) did not accept from them. Arbad then intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ), but Allah turned him away. He and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl set out heading for their people, and they agreed to bring the cavalry of Banu 'Amir against the Prophet (ﷺ). Then Allah destroyed Arbad with a thunderbolt that struck him, and destroyed 'Amir with a boil that grew on his body, of which he died in the house of a woman from Banu Salul on his way to the land of his people. So [the words] ﴿and He sends the thunderbolts﴾ were revealed concerning Arbad, and [the words] ﴿while they dispute about Allah﴾ concerning 'Amir.

[p. 107]

Al-Tabari mentions from Suhar al-'Abdi that it was revealed concerning another tyrant. And from Mujahid: that it was revealed concerning a Jew who disputed about Allah, and a thunderbolt struck him.

Since 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl came to Madina only after the Hijra, and the disputation of the Jews could only occur after the Hijra, the transmitters of these reports ventured to say that the sūrah is Madinan, or that these verses among it are Madinan. These reports go back to the opinion of some people who speculate about the causes of revelation. No sound and explicit report has been established on this, so no reliance is placed on what they said, and it does not remove the sūrah from the category of Meccan sūrahs. In this story, 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl sent forth his saying, as a proverb: "A boil like the boil of a camel, and death in the house of a Salulite woman."

Labid ibn Rabi'a elegized his brother Arbad with verses, among which:

I fear for Arbad the calamities, and I do not dread the rain-star of al-Simak or of al-Asad.

The thunder and the thunderbolts have bereaved me of the horseman, on the day of the dreadful battle, the brave.
