Since 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl came to Madina only after the Hijra, and the disputation of the Jews could only occur after the Hijra, the transmitters of these reports ventured to say that the sūrah is Madinan, or that these verses among it are Madinan. These reports go back to the opinion of some people who speculate about the causes of revelation. No sound and explicit report has been established on this, so no reliance is placed on what they said, and it does not remove the sūrah from the category of Meccan sūrahs. In this story, 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl sent forth his saying, as a proverb: "A boil like the boil of a camel, and death in the house of a Salulite woman."

Labid ibn Rabi'a elegized his brother Arbad with verses, among which:

I fear for Arbad the calamities, and I do not dread the rain-star of al-Simak or of al-Asad.

The thunder and the thunderbolts have bereaved me of the horseman, on the day of the dreadful battle, the brave.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 14:

﴿To Him is the call of truth. And those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except like one who stretches out his hands toward water so that it may reach his mouth, but it will not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error.﴾

This is a fresh, initiating statement (isti'naf ibtida'i), placed as a conclusion and as the establishing of what was demonstrated by the preceding verses, which are proofs of His sole creation at the first origin and then the second creation, of His complete power to which no other power comes close, and of His all-encompassing knowledge. Therefore it is necessary that the possessor of these attributes is the one truly worthy of worship, and that worship of other than Him is error.

Al-da'wah (the call) means seeking to turn someone toward oneself. Its use has become common for seeking to turn someone toward oneself for help or for giving. This is specifically required when it is attributed to God, since true turning toward Him is impossible; so what is meant is seeking rescue or bounty.

The attribution of "the call" to "the truth" is either an attribution of a qualified noun to its qualifier, if al-haqq means "that which corresponds to reality," i.e., the call which accords with reality, meaning that He deserves it; or an attribution of a thing to its source, like the phrase "the brocades of Yemen," i.e., the call issuing from truth, which is the opposite of falsehood, since calling upon God issues from the belief in His oneness, which is the truth, while worship of idols issues from the belief in association, which is falsehood.

The lam here denotes figurative ownership, which is entitlement. Placing the prepositional phrase before the subject indicates restriction, i.e., the call of truth belongs to Him and not to the ownership of anyone else; this is a relative restriction (qasr idafi).

The clause "And those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them with anything" explicitly states the implication of the restrictive clause, so it serves as its elaboration. The apparent requirement would be to separate it without conjunction, but it was conjoined because of the comparison and illustration it contains, so it goes beyond the measure of mere elaboration. The purpose is to show that the idols do not deserve to be called upon by those who call. The relative pronoun applies to the idols. The pronoun in "yad'una" refers to the polytheists. The link of the relative clause is an elided object pronoun; the estimated reading is: "And those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them."

The pronoun of rational beings is applied to the idols in "do not respond" (la yastajibuna), in conformity with the common usage of the Arabs, since they treat the idols as though they were rational.

Al-istijabah is responding to the summons of the one who calls and the call of the one who invokes; the sin and ta' here intensify the verb.

The ba' in "bi-shay'" serves to transitivize "yastajibuna," since the verb of responding is transitive to the thing responded with by means of ba'. When the response is intended to mean achieving what is hoped for, it is used without an object, as in His saying: ﴿So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their plotting﴾ [Yusuf: 34].

Since what is intended here is negating any benefit from their calling upon the idols, the negation of response is made transitive by ba' to the negation of the least that a respondent may give, namely a promise of giving or an excuse for not giving. They are unable to do that, and they are even less able to do what is above it.

The indefinite "shay'" is for belittling. What is meant is the least of speech by which one may be answered.

The exception in "﴿except like one who stretches out his hands﴾" is from the generality of the states of the callers and the responders, and of the calling and the responding, since it is a comparison of a whole configuration, so it extends to all its parts. Thus one may estimate the sentence as: "except like a caller who stretches out," or "except like the state of one who stretches out." The meaning: they do not respond to them in any state of calling and responding, except in a state like that of one who stretches out his hands to water. This exception is from affirming a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, and it returns to negating response in all other states, by way of allusion and metaphor.

By "one who stretches out his hands" is meant one who scoops water with two open hands, not closed, since water does not stay in them. This is like saying: "He is like one who grasps water," as an image of wasting what is sought. Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

*So I became, regarding what was between me and her of affection, like one who grasps water in his hand.*

"Ila" denotes the endpoint, since the word "basit" indicates that he extended his two open hands toward the water. The lam in "liyabligha" returns to the water, and likewise the pronoun "huwa" and the pronoun attached in "bali-ghih" refer to the mouth.

The statement is an allegory. The state of the polytheists in calling upon the idols, seeking to bring them benefit, while the idols respond to them with nothing, is likened to the state of one parched with thirst who stretches out his hands seeking that the water rise in his two open hands to his mouth so that he may quench himself; but it will not reach his mouth through that effort, so his striving and toil go in vain, together with what it contains of allusion and metaphor, as we have mentioned.

The clause "﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾" is conjoined to the clause "﴿And those they call upon besides Him﴾," to encompass the state of the one called upon and the state of the caller. The previous clause clarified the helplessness of the one called upon to respond, and was followed by the allegory containing allusion and metaphor. This also included, by allusion, the frustration of the caller.

This second clause clarified the frustration of the caller by explicit statement after its clarification by allusion. Thus, through the difference of purpose and style, the conjunction is appropriate, and in its result the first clause is confirmed and established; the second serves as a summary conclusion detailing the first.

Al-dalal means perdition and loss. "Fi" denotes figurative location, to indicate firm establishment in the attribute, i.e., "nothing but one lost in a severe loss."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 15:

﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows [too], in the mornings and the evenings.﴾ It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14]. That is: to Him is the call of truth, and to Him prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and this is the emblem of divinity. As for the call, it is exclusively for the true one (al-haqqa) to the exclusion of the false. As for prostration, which is inclining toward the earth with the intention of submission, Allah alone is its absolute object, because the exalted beings and the believers in Allah prostrate to Him, while the polytheists do not prostrate to the idols nor to Allah the Exalted, though perhaps they prostrate to Allah in some circumstances.

The expression turned away from the pronoun of majesty to His proper name, the Exalted, in conformity with the preceding style at the opening of the primary themes.

The generality derived from the relative pronoun (man) is a customary generality, by which is meant the vast majority.

The purpose of (﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾) is to divide the conditions of those who prostrate. By willingness is meant being driven by one's own self, seeking nearness and closeness out of pure veneration and love of Allah. By unwillingness is meant compulsion at times of severity and need, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then when harm touches you, to Him you cry for help﴾ [al-Nahl: 53]. From this is the saying: "Your brother is compelled, not a hero," meaning he is forced to fight.

The intended meaning of unwillingness is not coercion and constraint, as some have explained it; that is far from the aim, as will come.

Shadows (zilal): plural of zill, which is the image of a body onto which light is reflected.

The pronoun refers to those in the heavens and the earth, restricted to those among them that are dense bodies possessing shadows, by restriction established by reason and custom. It is conjoined to (man): that is, whoever is in the heavens prostrates, and their shadows prostrate.

Al-ghuduww (mornings): the time at which people go out to their needs. It may be a verbal noun with an elided modifier, meaning "the time of the going out," or it may be the plural of ghadwa. Its plural has been reported as ghuduww, and this was discussed at the end of Surat al-A'raf.

Al-asal: plural of asil, which is the time of the sun's yellowing at the end of the evening. The purpose of mentioning both is to encompass all portions of the periods of shadow.

The meaning of the prostration of shadows is that Allah created them from accidents of earthly bodies; they are bound to the system by which the rays of the sun are reflected upon them and the rays terminate at the solidity of the earth's surface, so that the shadows fall upon the earth in the manner of one prostrating. Thus, if there are people who refuse to prostrate to Allah or leave it off, occupied with prostrating to idols, Allah has made their likeness a witness to Allah's entitlement to prostration toward Him, a symbolic testimony. Had Allah made the sun two suns facing each other equally, shadows would cease to exist; and had He made the surface of the earth transparent or shining like water, the shadow would not appear clearly. This is among the symbols of the craftsmanship that Allah brought into being, and He made it with a wondrous precision. He arranged the system of earthly existents as prepared for it in their creation, for converging wisdoms, among them that they be signs indicating His singularity in divinity and the need of created things for Him. He placed most of these signs in the human species, since their species is distinguished by ingratitude, unlike animals.

The purpose of this symbolic argument is to alert to the subtleties of Divine craftsmanship, how it came in a consistent order, each part indicating the others, as it has been said:

"In everything there is a sign that indicates He is the One."

The argument, moreover, is that things prostrate to Allah, since their shadows fall upon the earth in every place, and they are not places of prostration to idols; and that the idols have specific locations which are their sanctuary and precinct. Most idols are in houses, such as al-'Uzza, Dhu al-Khalasa, and Dhu al-Ka'abat, where shadows vanish within houses.

This verse is a place of prostration among the prostrations of the Qur'an; it is the second prostration in the order of the mushaf by the agreement of the jurists. Among the wisdom of prostrating upon its recitation is that the Muslim places himself among those who prostrate to Allah willingly, by performing the prostration. This is a practical acknowledgment of servitude to Allah the Exalted.

[Page 113]

﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: God. Say: Have you then taken, apart from Him, protectors who possess neither benefit nor harm for themselves?﴾

When the clear proofs, drawn from the manifest varied existents, had established His sole divinity, through His words (﴿God is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]) and His words (﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]) and His words (﴿God knows what every female carries﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8]) and His words (﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12]) and the verses that follow, and through the subtle symbolic indications in them, from His words (﴿To Him is the true call﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14]) and His words (﴿And to God prostrates whoever is in the heavens﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]) to the end of them, the situation was indeed set for establishing the polytheists' affirmation in a way that left them no escape from acknowledgment. Then came the rebuke for their polytheism, a rebuke that left them no choice but to swallow its bitterness. For this reason the discourse was resumed and opened with the command to speak, to signal the clarity of the argument.

[Page 113 continues]

Because the interrogation is not genuine (*haqiqi*), its answer came from the questioner himself. This is common in the Qur'an and is one of its wondrous styles, as in His words (﴿About what do they question one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1]) (﴿About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 2]). It was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He, (﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God. He has prescribed mercy upon Himself﴾ [al-An'am: 12]) in Surat al-An'am.

The repetition of the verb of speech "say" in (﴿Say: Have you then taken...﴾), which is a consequence of the acknowledgment that God is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, is for the purpose of emphasizing that consequence because of the clear argument it contains.

So the interrogation is affirmation, reproach, and a declaration of their opinion as foolish, based on the acknowledgment they had conceded. It also contains another argument against the inability of their idols to be divine, for their taking them as protectors apart from Him is known and does not need to be asked about.

The clause (*la yamlikun*, "they possess not") is a qualifier (*sifah*) of (*awliya'*, "protectors"). Its purpose is to draw the attention of the listeners to consider that attribute. If they reflect, they will know it, and they will know that whoever has such an attribute is not fit to be worshipped.

The meaning of possession (*al-mulk*) here is power (*al-qudrah*), as in His words, exalted is He, (﴿Say: Do you worship, apart from God, what possesses for you neither harm nor benefit?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76]) in Surat al-'Uqud (al-Ma'idah). And in a hadith: "Can I possess for you [the power] that God should remove mercy from your heart?"

The conjunction of harm (*darr*) with benefit (*naf'*) is an exhaustive statement of their incapacity, since harm is by nature easier to bring about and more within reach.

[Page 114]

﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike? Or are the darknesses and the light alike?﴾

The repetition of the command to say is for the special emphasis on this speech, because what preceded it was a refutation of their gods' entitlement to worship. This is a demonstration of the superiority of those who believe in God over the polytheists. His words (﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: God﴾) implied that the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, called to the singling out of God in lordship, and that the addressees affirmed lordship for the idols. So their situation and his situation were like that of the blind and the seeing, and like that of the darknesses and the light.

The negation of equality between the two states implies a comparison with the two states, and this is one of the forms of eloquent simile (*al-tashbih al-baligh*).

"Am" (*am*) here is a transitional *idrab* (a shift to another matter) in the simile, so it is for another comparison, like the word "or" (*aw*) in the verse of Labid:

"Or the renewed tracing of a tattooed woman, whose dye has been worn away,"

and His words, exalted is He, (﴿Or like a downpour from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]). The particle "hal" (*hal*, "whether") was made explicit after "am," because it conveys the confirmation of the interrogation. This is not something in which the meaning of "am" alone suffices to express the basic interrogation. For this reason the hamzah of interrogation does not appear after "am," being satisfied with the indication of "am" that an interrogation is implied.

The plural of "darknesses" and the singular of "light" were discussed earlier at His words, "And He made the darknesses and the light" [al-An'am: 1], at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

The comparison was chosen among the opposites, blindness and sight, darkness and light, for complete suitability. The state of the polytheists, who are the people of blindness, is like the state of darkness in the absence of perceiving

[Page 115]

visible things, and the state of the believers is like the state of sight in knowledge and like the state of light in bestowing guidance and direction.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read (﴿Are the darknesses...﴾, *tastawi al-zulumat*) with a *ta'* (feminine prefix) at its beginning, in consideration of the feminine gender of "darknesses." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf read it with a *ya'* (masculine prefix) at its beginning, and this is a permissible option for a plural that is not a masculine sound plural.

﴿Or have they set up for God partners who create as He creates, so that the creation seemed alike to them? Say: God is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer.﴾

"Am" here is a transitional *idrab* in the interrogation, corresponding to His words (﴿Have you then taken, apart from Him, protectors who possess neither benefit nor harm for themselves?﴾). So the speech after "am" is an interrogation whose particle has been omitted, because "am" indicates it. The estimated form is: (﴿Or have they set up for God partners?﴾). The address turned away from second person to third person, as a turning away from them because of their misguidance already mentioned.

The interrogation is used for mockery and confusion. The meaning is: if they had set up for God partners who create as God creates, they would have had some excuse for being deceived and for taking them as gods. That is, they have no excuse for their worship. So the clause (*khalaqu*, "they create") is a qualifier of (*shuraka'*, "partners").

The prepositional phrase (*ka-khalqihi*, "as His creation") has the sense of an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*): they created a creation like what God created. The noun "creation" (*khalq*) is a verbal noun in both places.

The clause (*fa-tashabaha*, "so that ... seemed alike") is conjoined to the clause (﴿they created as His creation﴾), so it is a second qualifier of (*shuraka'*). The link is the definite article in (*al-khalq*, "the creation"), since it is a substitute for the pronoun suffixed to it. The estimate is: "so their creation seemed alike to them." The two qualifiers are the target of the mockery and confusion.

The clause (﴿Say: God is the Creator of all things﴾) is a summary of what came before and a conclusion from it. When the reproachful interrogation came in (﴿Have you then taken... protectors?﴾) and in (﴿Or have they set up for God partners who created as His creation?﴾), it was such that it results in: those whom they took as partners of God, and whose deficiency in possessing benefit or harm for themselves has been shown, and who do not create as God creates, are only creatures of God, exalted is He; God is the Creator of all things; and those idols are only things included in the generality of "all things." God is the One who is unique in creation, and the Subduer of everything other than Him. The object of unity and the object of subjugation were omitted because their referent is determined. The estimate is: "the One in creation, the Subduer of the existents."

Subjugation (*al-qahr*) means overpowering. It was discussed at His words, exalted is He, (﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 18]) in Surat al-An'am.

[Page 117]

The clause ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾ is an initial resumptive statement (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), which records the deprivation of the polytheists from benefiting from the proofs of guidance that by their nature would guide anyone whose heart Allah has not sealed, and by which the believers were guided.

In this record, the manner of presenting a parable (*darb al-mathal*) is used, by means of two groups' reactions to one and the same thing: one group benefited from its benefits, and another clung to its harms. In this parable is a condition that indicates the wondrous disposal of Allah the Exalted, so that the discourse may pass (*takhallus*) from mention of the proofs of power to mention of lessons of admonition. Thus the whole construction is used in the figurative comparison (*al-tashbih al-tamthili*), with the indication of His saying ﴿Thus Allah strikes the truth﴾ and so on.

The sending down of the Qur'an, by which there is guidance, is compared to the sending down of water from the sky, by which there is benefit and life. The arrival of the Qur'an upon people's hearing is compared to a torrent that passes over various directions: it passes over hills and mountains and does not settle in them, but proceeds to the valleys and depressions, and each takes from it according to its capacity. And those torrents, in the state of their descent, carry at their crests foam, which is the froth of water that swells and floats upon the surface of the water. So the foam goes away, unbenefited, and the pure clear water remains, from which people benefit for drinking and irrigation.

Then the form of the descent of the verses, and what they contain of awakening attention to them, is compared: whoever has faith entering his heart benefits from them according to the degree of the strength of his faith and his deeds; and they pass over the hearts of a people who do not perceive them, namely the deniers and those who turn away; and they mix with the hearts of a people who ponder them, and so take from them what stirs up for them doubts and heresy, such as their saying ﴿Shall we show you a man who tells you, when you have been torn to pieces completely, that you will indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [Saba': 7]. Of this also is the taking of the ambiguous (*al-mutashabih*), as He the Exalted said ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7].

All of that is compared to the form of the descent of water: its pouring down upon mountains and hills, and its flowing in valleys according to their differing capacities, then what it casts out of itself of foam that is not benefited from. Then the foam did not remain long before it went away and perished, while the water remained in the earth for benefit.

Since the intended thing is the comparison with the whole form, the narration of what resulted from the sending down of water is connected by the particle of consequence (*fa'* of sequence, *tafri'*) in His saying ﴿so it flowed﴾ and His saying ﴿so the torrent carried﴾. This is an allegory suitable for dividing the comparisons of which it is composed, and it is the most eloquent kind of allegory.

In the manner of this allegory and its explanation came what the Prophet ﷺ clarified in the allegory he said: "The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which Allah sent me is like abundant rain that fell upon a land; some of it was pure ground which accepted the water and produced grass and abundant herbage; and some of it was hard ground which held the water, and Allah benefited people by it, so they drank, gave drink, and planted; and it fell upon another part which was but barren plains that hold no water and produce no herbage. That is the likeness of one who comprehends the religion of Allah and is benefited by what Allah sent me with, so he knows and teaches; and the likeness of one who does not raise his head to it and does not accept the guidance of Allah with which I was sent."

*Al-awdiya* is the plural of *al-wadi*, which is the wide, extended depression of the earth in which the torrent flows. It has been mentioned earlier in Surat Bara'ah at His saying ﴿nor do they cross a valley except that it is recorded for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 121].

*Al-qadar* is with two fathas. His saying ﴿according to its measure﴾ (*bi-qadarih*) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) relating to *awdiyah*. He mentioned it because it is one of the places of lesson, namely that the channels of the valleys are in proportion to what they can hold of torrents, such that they do not overflow over them, and this is the usual state of valleys. This circumstance is intended in the allegory, because it is the state of water being directed to a benefit with no harm accompanying it, for among torrents there are destructive floods that sweep away crops, houses and livestock.

Also, it indicates the differing capacities of valleys with respect to water quantities. This has a share of the comparison, namely the people's differing readiness to benefit from what came down from Allah, like the differing of valleys in accepting water according to what flows to them from the outlets of torrents. The allegory is complete at this point.

The clause ﴿And from what they kindle in the fire, seeking an ornament or goods, there is foam like it﴾ is an interjected clause between the clause ﴿so the torrent carried foam, swelling﴾ and the clause ﴿As for the foam﴾.

This is another allegory, introduced as a digression after the mention of its counterpart, serving to bring the allegory closer to a people who had not witnessed the torrents of the valleys, such as the people of Makkah, who are the intended audience. For they had goldsmiths in Makkah, as the hadith of the *idhkhir* indicates. So the Qur'an brought near to them the allegory of the non-benefit from what others benefited from, by the likeness of what is smelted of gold and silver in crucibles, for it casts off foam which is removed from it, namely the dross, which is useless for anything at the very time when its metal is fit for being made into an ornament or goods. In the hadith: "As the bellows removes the dross of iron."

So the discourse is of the kind of multiplying a close comparison, like His saying ﴿Their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], then His saying ﴿or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19].

Closer to what is here is the words of Labid:

*"They contended over a smooth-running torrent whose shade flies up, like the smoke of a kindled fire whose blaze flares up,*

*mixed, perfumed with a plant of 'arfaj, its humps (?) like the smoke of a blazing fire."*

What conveyed this in this verse is His saying ﴿foam like it﴾.

The fronting of the predicate over the subject in this clause is for the sake of drawing attention to the predicate, because it is also a place of contemplation of the wondrous making of Allah the Exalted, for He made the foam float upon the thinnest of bodies, which is water, and upon the thickest of them, which is the metal. So it is one of the laws of creation. By the fronting, the listener's expectation is aroused to await the subject.

This emphasis on the comparison resembles the emphasis by interrogation in the words of the Prophet ﷺ describing Hell: "There are hooks in it like the thorns of the sa'dan thistle. Have you seen the thorns of the sa'dan?"

He turned away from naming gold and silver to the relative construction with His saying ﴿from what they kindle in the fire﴾, because it is more concise and comprehensive, and because the purpose in mentioning the clause made into a relative clause (*silah*) is that if it had been mentioned in a manner other than a relative clause, such as an adjectival description for instance, it would have been like a superfluous element in the speech, and the speech would have been lengthened by naming the two metals along with the relative clause, since there is no escape from mentioning the fuel, for it is the cause of the foam. So bringing the relative pronoun was fulfilling the right of mentioning the clause together with brevity that is wondrous.

And because in turning away from naming gold and silver there is an aversion that signals little concern with them, a elevating oneself above people's infatuation with them, since their names have been associated with glorification in people's usage.

The *min* in His saying ﴿from what you kindle﴾ is for origin (*ibtida'iyyah*).

The phrase ﴿seeking an ornament or goods﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*) related to ﴿you kindle﴾. It is mentioned to clarify the intended meaning of the relative clause and to incorporate in it the favour of subjecting these things to people, because of their strong desire for them.

*Al-hilyah* is what one adorns oneself with, that is, what is beautified, and it is the wrought (metal). *Al-mata'* is what one enjoys and benefits from, and that is the minted coin which people deal in, of gold and silver.

The majority read ﴿you kindle﴾ with a *fawqiyyah* (second-person) at its beginning, as address. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, and Khalaf read it with a *tahtiyyah* (third-person) as absence.

The clause ﴿Thus Allah strikes the truth and the falsehood﴾ is an interjected clause. It is the concluding summary (*fadhlakah*) of the allegory by stating its purpose, that is: a parable like this state is the striking of a parable for truth and falsehood. So the meaning of *yadribu* ("strikes") is "clarifies and illustrates." The meaning of *yadribu* has already been discussed at His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is not ashamed to strike an example﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

So a noun has been omitted in His saying ﴿Allah strikes the truth﴾, and the estimate is: Allah strikes the parable of truth and falsehood, because the verb *yadribu* indicates this omitted noun.

The omission of the preposition from *al-haqq* is for treating the noun in the genitive as if it were the omitted noun in the construct phrase.

It has been established that the foam is a parable for falsehood and the water is a parable for truth. Then he rose at this point to what the two parables contain of the attributes of permanence and passing away, so as to reach by that the good news and warning for the people of truth and the people of falsehood: that the first group is the enduring and everlasting, and the second group is transient and perishing. Like His saying ﴿And We have written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105], and ﴿Indeed in this is a message for a people who worship﴾. So the comparison became an allusion and a metonymy for good news and warning, as His saying after it indicates: ﴿For those who responded to their Lord is the best; and those who did not respond to Him﴾ [al-Ra'd: 18], and so on, as will come shortly.

So the clause ﴿As for the foam﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿so the torrent carried foam, swelling﴾, branching from the allegory. It is introduced by *amma* for emphasis and for directing the listener's mind to the speech containing hidden good news and warning, and because it completes the allegory. The estimate is: "So the foam went away as rubbish, and what benefits people remained in the earth."

*Al-juffa'* is what is cast out and thrown away. This is a threat to the polytheists that they will be annihilated by killing, and the believers will remain.

What benefits people is used to express the water, to point to the reason for the construction of the predicate, which is remaining in the earth, as an allusion to the polytheists that they should examine their conditions against the content of this relative clause, so that they may know that they are not among those who benefit people. This relative clause balances the description in His saying ﴿that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105].

Mention is sufficient of the aspect of resemblance of what benefits to water, and what does not benefit to foam, instead of mentioning the aspect of resemblance of what benefits to gold or silver and what does not benefit to their foam, being content without it.

The clause ﴿Thus Allah strikes the parables﴾ is a resumed concluding statement (*tadhyil*, a concluding generalization) for what is in the word "parables" of generality. It is more general than the clause ﴿Thus Allah strikes the truth and the falsehood﴾, since it indicates one kind of parable and not all of its kinds. So when it was followed by another parable, namely ﴿As for the foam, it goes away as rubbish﴾, the attention was directed to the general benefit of striking parables. Also there was achieved an emphasis of the clause ﴿Thus Allah strikes the truth and the falsehood﴾, because the particular is included in the general.

The demonstrative *dhalika* ("thus") refers to the preceding allegory in the clause ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning: like that wondrous mode of striking, Allah strikes the parables, and this is the intended meaning of this concluding statement.

The demonstration serves to highlight that parable and to draw the understanding to its wisdom and the wisdom of the allegory, and the admonitions and lessons in it, and what it gathers of allegory and allusive metonymy, and to the eloquence of the Qur'an and its inimitability. This is a delight to the believers and a challenge to the polytheists. And so it may be known that the clause ﴿As for the foam, it goes away as rubbish﴾ was not brought merely to exhibit the subtleties of divine power and wondrous making, but also to strike a parable, so that the one represented is known by way of allusion regarding the polytheists and the believers. Thus the speech is complete at His saying ﴿Thus Allah strikes the parables﴾, as is the nature of a concluding statement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 18:

﴿For those who respond to their Lord is the best (reward). As for those who do not respond to Him, [even] if they had everything on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom. Those will have the terrible reckoning, and their refuge will be Hell, and wretched is the resting-place.﴾

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) following the phrase ﴿Thus does Allah strike the examples﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]. That is, the benefit of these examples is that for those who respond to their Lord, when He strikes them for them, there is the best (reward), and so on to the end.

Its connection to the two parables mentioned earlier is that both of them refer to the conditions of the Muslims and the polytheists. In mentioning this sentence there is added emphasis on the parable and its purpose, along with the recompense of both groups. For the believers responded to Allah by understanding the examples, so they were rewarded with the best, whereas the polytheists turned away and did not understand the examples. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And none understands them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. So their recompense was a great punishment, namely the terrible reckoning, whose outcome is the destination of Hell. The meaning of ﴿they responded to their Lord﴾ is that they responded to His call with what the preceding example and others contained.

The phrase al-husna (the best) is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿for those who responded﴾ is its predicate (khabar). In the shift to the two relative pronouns with their relative clauses in His saying ﴿for those who responded﴾ and ﴿and those who did not respond to Him﴾, there is an indication that the two relative clauses are the causes of what befell the two groups.

The predicate is fronted in His saying ﴿for those who responded to their Lord is the best﴾ because it is the more important, since the purpose is to honour the status of those who responded, while placing al-husna in the position of the subject also honours it.

As for the report about the threat to those who did not respond, it has been left in the original arrangement of speech regarding fronting and postponement, owing to the little concern for them. The like of His saying ﴿even if they had everything on earth and the like of it with it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 36] has already been mentioned in Surat al-'Uqud.

The demonstrative noun was used in ﴿Those will have the terrible reckoning﴾ to draw attention to the fact that they deserve what follows the demonstrative as the predicate, because of what precedes the demonstrative as the relative clause.

The "terrible reckoning" (su' al-hisab) is what surrounds the reckoning of harshness and humiliation toward the one being reckoned. As for the essence of reckoning itself, it is good, because it is justice.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 19:

The speech, in the form of a question, aims at negating the equality of the believer and the disbeliever, as an alert to the heedlessness of the astray regarding the non-equality (of the two), like His saying ﴿Is he who was a believer like he who was a defiant sinner? They are not equal﴾ [al-Sajdah: 18].

The name of the blind (a'ma) is borrowed for one who does not know that the Qur'an is the truth, because his knowledge of an evident, clear thing has been negated, so he resembles the blind man. The kaf (in "kaman") for similarity (tashabbuh) is used in the sense of equivalence (tamathul). The equality intended here is equivalence in merit (fadl), by the indication of the mention of blindness. This sentence has a connection in meaning with His saying at the beginning of the surah ﴿And those to whom what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1], up to ﴿they do not believe﴾.

The restriction by (innama) is relative (idafi), i.e., (it means) only the people of understanding and not others. It is thus an allusion (ta'rid) against the polytheists, that they have no intellects, since the benefit of their intellects has been removed from them.

**[Page 125]**

The phrase ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of God and do not break the pact﴾, through to ﴿and those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord, establish the prayer, spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good; for them is the good end of the abode﴾, may be a new statement (*istiʾnaf ibtidaʾi*), which has come because of what the preceding sentence conveys, namely the denial of equality between two groups. For this reason, the states of the two groups are mentioned in these sentences, in terms of praiseworthy and blameworthy qualities, so that it becomes clear that the negation of equality between them in the previous sentence, the negation whose purpose is to prefer one of the two groups over the other, is supported by proof. In this way, the position of this sentence becomes one that gives the reason for the negation of equality, the purpose of which is to prefer the believers over the polytheists. Thus, ﴿Those who fulfil﴾ is the predicate of the subject, and so is what is conjoined to it. The sentence ﴿for them is the good end of the abode﴾ is the predicate.

The use of the demonstrative ﴿those﴾ (*ulaʾika*) in ﴿those, for them is the good end of the abode﴾ serves to alert the hearer that those referred to deserve what follows the demonstrative because of the qualities that precede it, as in the Almighty's words ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ (2:5) at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

A parallel to this sentence is the Almighty's words ﴿Those who are gathered on their faces to Hell, those are worse in place and further astray in way﴾ (25:34), which follows His words ﴿And they do not come to you with an example but that We bring you the truth and better explanation﴾ (25:33).

**[Page 126]**

It has become clear through this whole sentence and its position that it prefers those who know that what was revealed is the truth, on account of the qualities of perfection that they possess, which necessitate excellence in this world and a good destination in the Hereafter. It also (prefers them) over their opposites, who have the contrary of that, in the Almighty's words ﴿And those who break the covenant of God﴾ (13:25) up to His words ﴿and for them is the evil abode﴾ (13:25).

Fulfilling a covenant (*al-wafaʾ bi-l-ʿahd*) means that a person carries out what he has pledged to do. The meaning of *ʿahd* (covenant) is a firm promise, accompanied by showing the determination to carry it out, whether by an oath or by emphasis.

It is possible that ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of God﴾ is a qualifying description (*naʿt*) of the phrase ﴿people of understanding﴾ (*ulu al-albab*), and the sentence ﴿those, for them is the good end of the abode﴾ is a second qualifying description. The use of the demonstrative serves the purpose mentioned just above.

The phrase *ʿahd Allah* (the covenant of God) is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) with its object added to it, meaning what they pledged to God to do. Or it is an annexation of the verbal noun to its agent, meaning what God has enjoined upon them. In both cases, what is meant is the faith (*al-iman*) that God took from creation, referred to in the Almighty's words ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes"﴾ (7:172), which was mentioned in Surat al-Aʿraf. That is their covenant with their Lord. Also (it is referred to) in the Almighty's words ﴿Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy. And that you worship Me﴾ (36:60), and that is God's covenant with them, that they worship Him and not worship other than Him. Thus the covenant is established both by its annexation to its object and by its annexation to its agent.

That is a matter which God deposited in the innate nature (*fitrah*) of mankind, so their origin grew upon it, and their descendants bore it as a duty, and their acknowledgment that God is their creator continued. That is one of the effects of the covenant of God. Afterwards, the distortion of their covenant occurred; they began to forget, and matters became confused for some of them, so polytheism (*al-ishrak*) came upon them, due to their neglect of reflection upon the proofs of divine oneness (*tawhid*). Moreover, God has, through that covenant, deposited in the innate nature of sound minds the proofs of His oneness for whoever reflects and submits to the proof. But the polytheists turned away and were obstinate

**[Page 127]**

about that covenant established in the innate nature. Therefore, polytheism is necessarily a nullification of the covenant and a breaking of it. For this reason the clause ﴿and do not break the pact﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿fulfil the covenant of God﴾.

The definite article in *al-mithaq* (the pact) is taken as the definite article of the genus, so it encompasses all pacts. In this way it is more general than "the covenant of God," and so includes the pacts made between people, both agreements and oaths.

On account of this generality there arises a difference between it and the covenant of God. This difference justifies the conjunction of ﴿and do not break the pact﴾ to ﴿fulfil the covenant of God﴾, along with the emphasis on the meaning of the first by negating its opposite, and an allusion (*taʿrid*) against the polytheists, who are characterised by the opposite of that perfection. Thus the emphasis is conjoined on the basis of the difference between general and specific.

*Al-mithaq* and *al-ʿahd* are synonyms. *Al-iwfaʾ* (fulfilling) and the negation of breaking (*naqḍ*) have one meaning. The quality of this trait was mentioned first among the qualities because it indicates faith, and faith is the source and path of all good. For this reason the phrase ﴿and do not break the pact﴾ is conjoined to ﴿fulfil the covenant of God﴾, as a warning against everything in which the pact is broken.

These relative clauses (*ṣilat*) are qualities of the people of understanding, so their conjunction is of the type of conjoining qualities to a single described subject, not of conjoining categories. This is like the conjunction in the verse of the poet which al-Farraʾ cited in his *Maʿani al-Qurʾan*:

"To the lordly king and the son of the noble, and the lion of the battalion in the crush."

The meaning is: those who are characterised by the content of each of these relative clauses, whenever there arises a cause for them to be so characterised. So that when the cause exists and they do not act according to its requirement, they are not characterised by those virtues. Among them are some that necessitate being characterised by the opposite, and some that necessitate only neglect of excellence.

This relative pronoun, ﴿those﴾, and what is conjoined to it of relative pronouns, is repeated to indicate that its relative clauses are great qualities that necessitate attention to mentioning the one who is characterised by them, and to remove the supposition that the good end of the abode will be theirs only if they combine all these qualities.

**[Page 128]**

Therefore, what is meant by ﴿those who join what God has commanded to be joined﴾ is what applies to the group who fulfil the covenant of God. The reason for its conjunction is that joining what God has commanded to be joined is one of the effects of fulfilling the covenant of God, and that is the covenant of obedience, included in the Almighty's words ﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path﴾ (36:61) in Surat Ya Sin.

*Al-wasl* (joining) is the combining of one thing with another, and its opposite is severance (*al-qaṭʿ*). It is used metaphorically for nearness, and its opposite is abandonment (*al-hajr*). It is also well known metaphorically for kindness and honouring, and from this comes the saying *ṣilat al-rahim* (maintaining the ties of kinship), meaning kindness for the sake of the womb, that is, for the sake of kinship arising from the wombs, directly or indirectly, and that relationship is derived from the mothers. It is also applied to blood kinship from the side of the fathers, because it is generally not free of sharing a mother, even if remote.

The phrase ﴿what God has commanded to be joined﴾ is general to all bonds and ties which God has commanded to be shown love and kindness towards their owners. Among them is the bond of faith, and among them is the bond of kinship, which is maintaining the ties of kinship. The commentators have agreed that the latter is what God means here. A similar expression has already occurred in the Almighty's words ﴿and He does not lead astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient﴾ (2:26), and ﴿those who break the covenant of God after its confirmation and sever what God has commanded to be joined﴾ (2:27), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The expression about it was elaborated by the relative pronoun construction ﴿what God has commanded to be joined﴾ (13:25) because of what the relative clause contains of an allusion that the one who joins it is doing what pleases God, so that the discourse moves from that to an allusion against the polytheists who severed the bonds of kinship between themselves and the Messenger of God ﷺ and those with him among the believers, and who harmed them in every condition, and who wrote the document of boycott against the Banu Hashim.

In it is also praise of the believers for joining the wombs (kinship ties), and for not severing the kinship ties of their polytheist people except when those people waged war against them and opposed them.

**[Page 129]**

The phrase ﴿to be joined﴾ (*an yuwṣal*) is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *bihi*, meaning what God has commanded to be joined. This construction was used to increase the affirmation of the intended meaning, which is the wombs (kinship ties), after affirming it through the relative pronoun.

*Al-khashyah* (fear) is fear accompanied by magnifying the one feared. It has already occurred in the Almighty's words ﴿And indeed, it is difficult except for the humble﴾ (2:45) in Surat al-Baqarah. It is also applied to fear in general.

*Al-khawf* (fear) is the expectation that harm will befall from something. It has already occurred in the Almighty's words ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of God﴾ (2:229) in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿The evil of the reckoning﴾ (13:18) is what surrounds it of things which are displeasing to the one who is reckoned. This has already been mentioned just above. That is, they fear that it will befall them, so they abandon evil deeds.

The relative clauses ﴿those who fulfil﴾ and ﴿those who join﴾, and what is conjoined to them, came in the present tense in those five verbs, to indicate renewal, as a metonymy for continuity.

The relative clause ﴿those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾, and what is conjoined to it, namely ﴿establish the prayer and spend﴾, came in the past tense, to indicate the certainty of these three actions for them and their firm establishment in themselves, honouring them, because they are the foundations of the excellent deeds.

As for patience (*al-sabr*), it is because it is the cornerstone (*milak*) of the uprightness of deeds and their source. When the believer is characterised by it, good deeds and virtues proceed from him with ease. For this reason the Almighty said ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds and enjoin one another to truth and enjoin one another to patience﴾ (103:2–3).

As for the prayer (*al-salah*), it is because it is the pillar of the religion, and it has in it what patience has of distinctive quality, as in the Almighty's words ﴿Indeed, the prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ (29:45), and His words ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ (2:45).

As for spending (*al-infaq*), its root is the zakat (obligatory alms), which accompanies the prayer whenever it is mentioned, and it has the greatest share of the religion's concern. It includes expenditures and all gifts. It is one of the most important deeds, because giving away wealth is difficult for the souls, so it had such importance that it was made second to the prayer.

**[Page 130]**

Then the verbal style returned to the present tense in the clause conjoined to the relative clause, namely the Almighty's words ﴿and repel evil with good﴾. The context requires indicating renewal, as a hint that the renewal of this repelling is something to be eagerly pursued, since people are exposed to evil deeds in varying degrees. So a remedy for that is described to them: that they repel evil deeds with good deeds.

The discussion regarding the conjunction of ﴿those who are patient﴾ and the repetition of the relative pronoun is the same as the discussion regarding ﴿those who join what God has commanded to be joined﴾.

Patience (*al-sabr*) is among the praiseworthy qualities. It has already occurred in the Almighty's words ﴿and seek help through patience﴾ (2:45) in Surat al-Baqarah. The intended meaning is patience in the face of the hardships of good deeds and of supporting the religion.

﴿Seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*) for ﴿were patient﴾. *Al-ibtigha'* (seeking) is seeking. The meaning of seeking the countenance of God is seeking His pleasure, as if one performs an action by which one seeks His favour at the time of meeting Him. It has already occurred in the Almighty's words ﴿And whatever you spend, you do not spend except seeking the countenance of God﴾ (2:272) at the end of Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning is that they were patient because patience is commanded by God, not for another purpose such as showing off, so that it may be said "how patient he is under hardships," or to avoid the gloating of enemies.

The reason for mentioning secrecy and openness has already been explained in the Almighty's words ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾ (2:274) at the end of Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-daraʾ* means repelling and driving away. It is used here metaphorically for removing the effect of a thing, so it occurs after the occurrence of the thing repelled and before its occurrence, by preparing what prevents its occurrence. This is realised by following an evil deed, if it has been committed, with good deeds, for that is like driving away the evil deed. The Prophet ﷺ said: "O Muʿadh, fear God wherever you are, and follow an evil deed with a good deed, and it will erase it." This applies especially to what lies between a person and his Lord.

Ibn 'Ashur also holds that one should not answer an evil done to him with the same evil, but should respond with good. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better; then the one between you and whom there is enmity will become as though a devoted friend.﴾ [Fussilat 41:34] This means joining the one who cut you off, giving to the one who deprived you, and pardoning the one who wronged you. This applies between individuals and likewise between groups, so long as it does not lead to the continuation of harm. Allah the Exalted says concerning this: ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make reconciliation between your two brothers.﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:10]

He also holds that turning away from doing an evil after resolving on it is itself a good deed, which repels the evil that one had resolved upon. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever resolves to do an evil deed but does not do it, Allah records it for him as a good deed."

Thus [the verse] includes all of these meanings (yadra'un). For this reason it is not followed by anything that requires that the intended meaning is treating the wrongdoer with good, as was the case in His saying ﴿The good and the evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ [Fussilat 41:34] in Surat Fussilat, and as in His saying ﴿Repel evil with that which is best; We know best what they describe.﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:96] in Surat al-Mu'minun.

The clause ﴿those – for them is the final outcome of the abode﴾ is a predicate (khabar) about ﴿those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾. The demonstrative pronoun indicates that those referred to deserve the judgment stated after it, because of the attributes that were described for them. This is like His saying ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:5] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The prepositional phrase (majrur) was placed before the subject (mubtada') to indicate restriction (qasr), meaning: the final outcome of the abode is for them, not for those who possess the opposites of their attributes. This is a restriction of the relative (qasr idafi) type.

Al-'Uqba (the final outcome) means al-'aqiba, that which comes after (ya'qubu), i.e., which occurs following something else. Its use has become well known for a good end, as Allah the Exalted says ﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾ [al-A'raf 7:128] For this reason it is set here in contrast to its opposite in His saying ﴿and for them is the evil abode﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:25].

As for His saying ﴿and the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:35], it is a case of mushakala (rhetorical correspondence of wording), as will come at the end of the surah, at His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve will know for whom is the final outcome of the abode﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:42]. Refer also to what I mentioned in the explanation of His saying ﴿and whoever will have the good outcome of the abode﴾ [al-Qasas 28:37] in Surat al-Qasas, for I have expanded on it there.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 23–24:

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants. And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final abode!"﴾

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the final abode﴾, and 'adn (perpetual residence) means permanence (al-istiqrar). Its occurrence has already been discussed in His words ﴿and pleasant dwellings in gardens of 'Adn﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72] in Surat Bara'ah.

The mention of ﴿they will enter it﴾ serves to evoke the joyful state. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿gardens﴾ or to the pronoun in ﴿for them is the final abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22]. The waw in ﴿along with whoever was righteous among their fathers﴾ is the waw of accompaniment (waw al-ma'iyyah), and this is an increase in honor: He made their forefathers, their descendants, and their spouses, who are qualified to enter Paradise by virtue of their righteousness, join them in the rank they occupy. Whoever's rank is below theirs is joined to them, and whoever's rank is above theirs, they are joined to him, so the favor is theirs in both cases. This is like its reverse in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾ [al-Saffat: 22], etc., because witnessing the punishment of relatives is a doubled punishment.

In this verse there is good news for one who has a righteous predecessor, a righteous successor, or a righteous spouse, among those in whom these connections are realized: that when he enters Paradise, he will join the righteous among his forefathers, descendants, or spouse. God mentioned this only for this good news, as God, exalted is He, said, ﴿And those who believed, and whose descendants followed them in faith – We will join with them their descendants, and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾ [al-Tur: 21].

The term "fathers" (al-aba') includes mothers by way of prevalence (al-taghlib), as they say: "al-abawayn" (the two parents).

The clause ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ is coordinated (atf) with "they will enter it," so it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause. This is among their honors and the highlighting of their status, for the visits of God's messengers to them are a manifestation of His honoring them.

The mention of ﴿from every gate﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for the frequency of the angels' visits to them, to the extent that no gate of their houses is left without angels entering through it. That is because this entry, being a source of joy, is frequent in places. It is understood from this that it is frequent in times as well, so it is repeated, for they did not enter from every gate except because every gate is occupied by a group of them. It is as if it were said: "from every gate at every moment."

The ba' in ﴿for what you patiently endured﴾ is causal (lil-sababiyyah), and it is connected to the stable predicate derived from the prepositional phrase ﴿upon you﴾. The meaning is: this honor by peace has reached you because of your patience. It is also permissible that it be connected to an omitted element understood from the context, i.e., this bliss you witness is due to what you patiently endured.

The intended meaning is patience in the hardships of the obligations and in what they struggled with their wealth and their selves.

Upon this is built ﴿How excellent is the final abode!﴾, a consequence expressing praise for the goodness of their end, and the object of praise is omitted, being indicated by the context of address. The estimate is: "How excellent is the final abode, the abode of your end." The meaning of ﴿the final abode﴾ has already been explained above.

﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth - those will have the curse, and theirs will be the evil abode.﴾

This is an explanation of the state of the opposites of those who fulfil the covenant of Allah. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 26:

﴿Allah extends provision to whomever He wills, and straitens it. They rejoice in the worldly life, yet the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment.﴾

This sentence is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), answering what occurs to the minds of the listeners, both believers and disbelievers, upon hearing His words: ﴿For them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 25].

What it conveys is that they are the objects of divine wrath. As for the believers, they say: "How is it that Allah has extended provision to them in this world, so that they have only increased in transgression and disbelief? Why did He not punish them in this world with want, as He has decreed their punishment in the Hereafter?" This is like the words of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way﴾ [Yunus: 88]. As for the disbelievers, they mock the threat, boastful of the blessings they possess.

Both groups are answered: Allah wills to extend provision to some of His servants and to restrict it for others, for a wisdom connected with the means of livelihood in this world. And this has a connection with the state of honour with Him in the Hereafter. Hence the generality in His words "to whomever He wills" comes, and His will, exalted is He, and its causes, are not known to anyone.

The placing of the subject before the predicate verb in His words "Allah extends" (Allahu yabsutu) serves to strengthen the judgment and to emphasise it, because the intent is that people should know it and that minds be drawn to it, according to the view of al-Sakkaki regarding such constructions. The context is not one of restriction (qasr) as the Kashshaf adopted, since there is no one who claims a partner with Allah in this, nor one who claims that Allah does not do this such that a restrictive refutation is intended.

Al-Bast (extension): used metaphorically for abundance and continuity. Al-Qadr (restriction): a metonymy for scarcity.

Since the primary purpose of this discourse is to instruct the Muslims, the address is directed to them.

In the case of the disbelievers, the third-person pronoun is used, indicating that they are too inferior to grasp these subtleties, owing to the arrogance of their souls. They rejoiced in what they had in the worldly life and were heedless of the Hereafter. Thus the rejoicing mentioned is the rejoicing of insolence and transgression, as in His words, exalted is He, concerning Qarun: ﴿When his people said to him, "Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not love the exultant"﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. The meaning is: they rejoiced in the worldly life without concern for the Hereafter. This meaning is conveyed by the restriction to mention of the worldly life, while the Hereafter is also mentioned in His words ﴿and the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment﴾.

The intended meaning of "the worldly life" and "the Hereafter" is their bounties, by the indication of the context. So the speech is an attribution of a judgment to the essence while the intended meaning is its states.

"Fi" (in) is a stable adverbial phrase functioning as a circumstantial state (hal) of "the worldly life." The meaning of "fi" is the figurative sense of comparison, that is, when the states of the worldly life are compared with the states of the Hereafter, it becomes evident that the states of the worldly life are a little enjoyment. This was discussed earlier at His words ﴿Yet the enjoyment of the worldly life, in the Hereafter, is but little﴾ [al-Tawba: 38] in Surah Bara'a.

Al-Mata' (enjoyment): what is enjoyed and which passes away. Its indefiniteness is for minimisation, as in His words ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you; it is but a little enjoyment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 27:

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself those who turn back in repentance."﴾

One purpose is joined to another purpose, and one narrative to another. The connection lies in the mention of their rejoicing in the worldly life, for they were deceived by the provision they had, so they asked for the hastening of harm in their saying, ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. This sentence is a repetition of its earlier counterpart, ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. That sentence was repeated in the manner of an orator repeating a phrase from his sermon, so that he may bring what remains of that purpose after separating with what the situation required for separation, then return to what he had left before. For after the preceding verses had shown that Allah is able to hasten punishment for them, but His wisdom required not yielding to their demands, in order to challenge His servants, all of this was made fully clear. All of that is connected to His saying, ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5], and a return to the important matter of the purpose, which is to draw attention to the sign of the Qur'an and its indication of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). For this reason, the discussion on the guidance of the Qur'an was lengthened right after this sentence.

Therefore it is determined that the position of the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself those who turn back in repentance﴾ is the position of a statement used to express the Messenger's (ﷺ) amazement at the severity of their misguidance, such that whoever witnesses their state becomes certain that misguidance and guidance are in the hand of Allah, and that had they not been created with minds inclined to follow misguidance, they would have been guided, since the causes of guidance are clear.

Under this amazement there are other meanings:

The first: that the clear signs of the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) are evident, were it not that their minds did not perceive them due to the corruption of their perception.

The second: that clear sensory signs have come to other nations, and they saw them but did not believe. As Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And We did not refrain from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her with it﴾ [al-Isra': 59].

The third: that for their non-belief there are hidden causes known to Allah, which have been left ambiguous by making it conditional on His will in His saying, ﴿He leaves astray whom He wills﴾. Among them is what is hinted at in His saying in contrast to ﴿and guides to Himself those who turn back in repentance﴾. That is, they became arrogant and turned away when they heard the call to monotheism, so they did not reflect, though conclusive proofs had been presented to them, and they turned away from them. Had they turned back in repentance and submitted, Allah would have guided them, but they recoiled. By this, the position becomes clear of what the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to answer their saying, ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ by saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself those who turn back in repentance﴾, and that this is an allusion that they are among those whom Allah willed to be astray, and that their state is a cause of wonder.

As for repentance (inabah), its essential meaning is return. Here it is used for acknowledging the truth upon the manifestation of its proofs, because the soul initially recoils from the truth and then returns to it. Thus repentance here is the opposite of recoil.

﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is ṭūbā (a good state), and an excellent final return.﴾

It is a parenthetical resumptive sentence (*isti'nāf i'tirāḍī*), whose relevance lies in its contrast with the state of those whom Allah has led astray, and in its explanation of the state of those whom He has guided. It also alerts that the example of those who went astray is that their hearts do not find rest in the remembrance of Allah, which is the Qur'an, because their saying ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 27] implies that they did not regard the Qur'an as a sign from Allah. Then comes the explicit statement of the kind of outcome for these people, and the allusive indication of its opposite for those others. Thus mentioning it after the preceding sentence serves both purposes and points to the two causes.

For this reason, "those who believe" was not made a substitute (*badal*) for "whoever turns back (*man anāba*)", because if it were, the clause ﴿and their hearts find rest﴾ would not be conjoined to the relative clause, nor would "and do righteous deeds" be conjoined to the second relative clause. Rather, the first "those who believe" is the subject (*mubtada'*), the clause ﴿Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, the second "those who believe" is a corresponding apposition (*badal muṭābiq*) of the first, and the clause ﴿ṭūbā lahum﴾ is the predicate.

*Al-iṭmi'nān* means tranquility. It is used metaphorically here for certainty and the absence of doubt, since doubt is metaphorically described as agitation. It was discussed at His saying ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 260] in Surat al-Baqarah.

"The remembrance of Allah" may mean fear of Allah and watchfulness over Him by standing at His commands and prohibitions. It may also mean the Qur'an, as He says ﴿Indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 44], and this fits their saying ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 27], because they were not content with the Qur'an as a sign of the Messenger's truthfulness. On this meaning comes His saying in Surat al-Zumar ﴿Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Al-Zumar: 22], meaning to those whom hardness of heart had increased, and His saying at its end ﴿Then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Al-Zumar: 23].

[Page 138]

*Al-dhikr* is among the names of the Qur'an. It may also mean the remembrance of Allah with the tongue, since making it run on the tongue alerts the hearts to watchfulness over Him.

This is a description of the good state of the believers, set against the bad state of the disbelievers, whose hearts doubt has overwhelmed. He said ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 63].

The present tense *taṭma'innu* is chosen twice because it indicates the renewal of tranquility, its continuity, and that no doubt or hesitation intervenes.

The clause ﴿Surely in the remembrance of Allah﴾ is opened with the particle of alerting (*ḥarf al-tanbīh*), to emphasize its content and to urge attention to it. It serves as a concluding appendage (*tadhyīl*) to the generality conveyed by the definite noun "hearts". It also incites those who remain in disbelief to take on the mark of the believers, through reflection on the Qur'an so that their hearts may find rest, as if it said: If you know the ease of mind of the believers, what prevents you from being like them? That is within your reach, since the remembrance of Allah is within your hearing.

*Ṭūbā* is a verbal noun from *ṭāba ṭībān*, meaning it was good. It follows the pattern of *bushrā* and *zulfā*, and its *yā'* was changed to *wāw* for suitability to the *ḍamma*. The meaning is: for them is complete good, because their hearts found rest through the remembrance. Applying the term *ma'āb* to it is in view of it being the last of their affair and their settlement, just as a person's settlement is his house, to which he returns after dispersing from it. Moreover, it fits what is established, that souls are from the command of Allah, that is, from the realm of *malakūt*, which is the realm of eternity. Thus their destiny in eternity is a return to their first world. This is the counterpart of His saying about the polytheists ﴿and theirs is the evil abode﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 25].

The *lām* in His saying *lahum* is the *lām* of ownership (*li-l-milk*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 30:

Page 139
﴿Thus We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away, so that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you, while they disbelieve in the All-Merciful. Say: "He is my Lord; there is no god but He. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return."﴾

This is the answer to their saying ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27]. The earlier answer, with His saying ﴿Say: "Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27], was a response by turning away from their ignorance and expressing wonder at their misguidance, whereas what comes here is a response that rejects their saying. It is permissible to make this sentence part of the content of the saying (maqul al-qawl), and it is permissible to make it a separate sentence detached from the sentence ﴿Say: "Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27]. In either case, it stands as an explanation (bayan) of the whole sentence of saying, or an explanation of the content of the saying, which is wonder.

Its opening with His saying ﴿Thus (kadhalika)﴾, which is a demonstrative noun (ism ishara), serves to emphasize the thing pointed to, namely the wonder at their misguidance, since they were blind to the attribute of messengerhood.

The thing pointed to is the sending (al-irsal) derived from the verb ﴿We have sent you﴾, that is: like the clear sending, We have sent you. Thus the thing compared to is the same as the thing compared, indicating that because of its clarity it does not explain what is already clear in itself. A parallel to this has already occurred in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And thus We have made you a median community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Since the sending has been linked to His saying ﴿to a community before which other communities have passed away, so that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you﴾, the demonstrative also comes to carry the meaning of the sending of messengers before him to communities, which requires messengers. That is: your messengerhood was nothing but like the messengerhood of the messengers before you, as in His saying ﴿Say: I am not a novelty among the messengers﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9] and His saying ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20], in order to nullify the delusion of the polytheists that the Prophet ﷺ, since he did not bring them what they asked for, was not a messenger from Allah. In this argument there is a preparation for His saying ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains could be moved...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31].

For this reason the sentence is followed by His saying ﴿so that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you﴾.

The community (ummah) here is the community of the call (ummat al-da'wah), so among them are those who believed and among them are those who disbelieved.

The meaning of ﴿before which other communities have passed away﴾ has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran at His saying ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you ways (sunan)﴾. His saying ﴿before which other communities have passed away﴾ includes an allusion (ta'rid) with the threat of a fate like that of the earlier communities which denied their messengers.

The particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) in His saying ﴿so that you may recite to them﴾ implies that the sending is for the sake of guidance and direction through what Allah has commanded, not for the sake of displaying supernatural feats (kharq al-'adat).

Al-tilawah means recitation (al-qira'ah). So the intended meaning is: that you may read the Qur'an to them, as in His saying ﴿And that I should recite the Qur'an; so whoever is guided, is guided only for his own soul﴾ [al-Naml: 92], and so on.

In this there is an indication that the Qur'an is his miracle (mu'jizah), because He mentioned it in contrast to the sending of the earlier messengers and in contrast to His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾. This is stated explicitly in His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs such that people believed on account of them, but what I was given is a revelation (wahy) which Allah revealed to me." The sentence ﴿and they disbelieve in the All-Merciful﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon the sentence ﴿Thus We have sent you﴾, that is: We have sent you with the clearest guidance while they persist in disbelief, guidance having not entered their hearts. So the pronoun refers to the polytheists understood from the context, not to "a community," since some of the community are believers.

The use of the present tense in ﴿they disbelieve﴾ indicates the renewal and continuity of that. The meaning of their disbelief in Allah is their associating others with Him in divinity; thus they negated the reality of divinity, and so they disbelieved in Him.
