The choice of the name al-Rahman among His names, may He be exalted, is because their disbelief in this name is more severe, since they denied that Allah is Merciful (rahman). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the All-Merciful," they say: "And what is the All-Merciful?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 60] in Surat al-Furqan. So the verse points to two kinds of their disbelief: denial of unity (wahdaniyyah), and denial of the name al-Rahman. Also, because this attribute has a particular connection with their denial of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and with his being supported by the Qur'an, since the Qur'an is guidance and mercy for mankind. They wanted to substitute for it supernatural feats, which do not by their nature bring guidance, but which indicate the truthfulness of the one who brings them.

Al-Maqatil and Ibn Jurayj said: this verse was revealed concerning the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, when "they wanted to write the document of the treaty, and the Prophet ﷺ said to the scribe: 'Write: In the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful.' Suhayl ibn 'Amr said: 'We do not know al-Rahman except the lord of al-Yamamah,' meaning Musaylimah. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Write: In Your name, O Allah.'" But this is far-fetched, since the surah is Meccan, as has been mentioned earlier.

From Ibn 'Abbas: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh disbelievers when the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Prostrate to the All-Merciful," and they said: "And what is the All-Merciful?" So it was revealed.

The Prophet ﷺ was instructed to nullify their reported disbelief in a comprehensive way by saying: "He is my Lord." The pronoun "He" refers to al-Rahman considering the one named by this name, that is: the Named One is my Lord, and al-Rahman is His name.

His saying "there is no god but He" is a negation of their associating others with Him in divinity. This is among what Allah commanded His Prophet to say, so it is a precaution (ihtiras) against the reply to their saying: "Muhammad ﷺ calls to one Lord, yet he says: His Lord is Allah and His Lord is al-Rahman." So His saying "there is no god but He" is an informative statement from the side of Allah in the manner of an interjection (i'tirad).

The sentence ﴿In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return﴾ is a consequence (natijah) of His being one Lord. And because it is like a consequence of that, it is separated from the preceding sentence on account of the connection between them.

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases, "in Him" and "to Him," serves to convey the exclusivity (ikhtisas) of trust and return to Him: that is, not to other than Him, since when He is singular in lordship, trust is in Him, and since He is characterized by al-Rahmaniyyah, return is to Him, because His being merciful is a strong indication of His accepting the repentance of His servant.

Al-matab is a noun of place/time-form (masdar mimi) on the pattern maf'al, meaning repentance (al-tawbah), and it conveys emphasis (mubalaghah), because the original of mimi masdars is that they are nouns of time made a metonym for the verbal noun; then their use became common until they became like the explicit form.

Since al-matab includes the meaning of returning to what Allah commands, al-matab is governed by the preposition "ila" (to).

The original form is matabi, with the suffix of the first person pronoun (ya' al-mutakallim), so the ya' was deleted for lightness and the kasrah was kept as evidence of the deleted letter, just as it is deleted in the vocative noun annexed to the ya'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 31:

﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion, or the earth could be split asunder, or the dead could be made to speak! Rather, to Allah belongs the affair entirely. Have not those who believe despaired that, if Allah willed, He would have guided all mankind?﴾

It is permissible for this to be a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause "Thus We have sent you to a community," because the purpose of the clause being conjoined is that his message was no different from the messages of the other Messengers, peace be upon them, as indicated by the description "a community before which communities have passed away" [al-Ra'd: 30]. So the clause "And if only there were a Qur'an" would be a completion of the answer to their statement "Why was a sign not sent down to him from his Lord?" [al-Ra'd: 27].

It is also permissible for it to be a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) between the clause "He is my Lord" [al-Ra'd: 30] and the clause "Is He who stands over every soul" [al-Ra'd: 33], as will come there. It is also permissible for it to be reported by the saying (maḥkiyya bil-qawl), conjoined upon the clause "He is my Lord; there is no god but Him" [al-Ra'd: 30].

The meaning: if a book from the earlier scriptures had included more than guidance, so that it became a source for producing wonders, then this Qur'an would be likewise; but no such Qur'an exists. This Qur'an is not required to include that, since that is not among the customs of the divine books.

The answer to "law" (lau) is omitted, because the context indicates it. Omitting the answer of "law" is frequent in the Qur'an, as in His words "And if only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire" [al-An'am: 27] and His words "And if only you could see when the criminals hang their heads before their Lord" [al-Sajda: 12].

This conveys an allusive meaning of condemnation of them for the extreme of their misguidance, since they were not guided by the guidance of the Qur'an and its proofs; the situation being: if a Qur'an had commanded the mountains to move, the earth to split, and the dead to speak, this Qur'an would have achieved that. But that is not the business of books. It is in the manner of the verse of Ubayy ibn Salma in the Ḥamāsa:

"Had any one-hoofed creature flown before it, it would have flown; but it has not flown."

As for the reason these three things were singled out from among the supposed extraordinary feats, there is what al-Wahidi and al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas: the unbelievers of Quraysh, Abu Jahl and Ibn Abi Umayya, sat behind the Ka'ba, then sent to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "If you would widen the mountains of Makkah for us, moving them so that our land expands and we can farm it, for it is narrow; or bring Syria near to us, for we trade thereto; or bring out Qusayy, that we may speak with him."

This report may be supported by the fact that the proposal of speaking with the dead was repeated in the saying in Surat al-An'am: "And if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them" [al-An'am: 111]. So in mentioning these things there is an indication of their mockery.

On this basis, "the earth was split" (quṭṭiʿat bihi al-arḍ) means the distances of journeys were cut short, as in His words Exalted is He: "Your ties were indeed severed" [al-An'am: 94].

The clause "Rather, to Allah belongs the affair entirely" is conjoined upon "And if only there were a Qur'an" by the particle of retraction (iḍrāb). That is: such is not the business of books; rather, to Allah belongs the command over every created thing. He is the One who sent down the Book, and He is the One who creates wonders if He wills; that is not up to the Prophet ﷺ nor at your demand. So Allah commanded His Prophet to say this speech, as a way of responding to their speech contrary to their intention, according to the method of the wise style (al-uslub al-ḥakīm). For they intended by what they said only mockery, so their speech was taken contrary to their intention, as an alert that it would be better for them to consider whether there was in the earlier books a Qur'an capable of producing what they asked for.

Similar to this is al-Ḥajjaj's saying to al-Qab'thara: "I will surely make you ride the adham," meaning the shackle. Al-Qab'thara answered him, saying: "Someone like the Amir carries on the adham and the ashhab," and turned it to the color of a horse.

The "command" here is the creative disposal (al-taṣarruf al-takwīnī); that is: neither the Qur'an nor anything else brings about any of what you asked for; rather Allah is the One who brings things into being.

The two conjoined clauses and the one they are conjoined upon convey the sense of restriction (qaṣr), because conjunction with "bal" is one of the means of restriction. The lām in "the affair" (al-amr) is for comprehensiveness (istighrāq), and "jamīʿan" is an emphasis on it. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject is merely for emphasis, since the restriction has been conveyed by "bal" the conjunctive.

Consequent upon the two clauses is the rhetorical interrogative "Have not those who believe despaired that, if Allah willed, He would have guided all mankind?", a denial of the absence of despair among those who believe; that is, they are worthy of ceasing their despair and of knowing that if Allah willed He would have guided all mankind.

In this speech is an additional affirmation of the content of the clause "Say: Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back" [al-Ra'd: 27].

"Yaʾsa" here means "to be certain" and "to know"; this verb is not used except with the "that" of the verbal noun (anna al-maṣdariyya). Its root derives from "al-yaʾs" (despair), which is the certainty of the non-attainment of the sought object after searching; it was then used for absolute certainty by way of metonymy (majāz mursal) through the relation of necessity, since the meaning of despair includes the meaning of knowledge, and this became common until it became a literal usage. Among its instances is the saying of Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi:

"I say to them at the mountain pass when they seize me: did you not know that I am the son of the knight Zahdam?"

And there are other examples.

It has been said that using "yaʾisa" in the sense of "knew" is the dialect of Hawazin, or the dialect of Banu Wahbil, a clan of al-Nakha'; it was named after a grandfather. But there is nothing compelling toward this. This is when "that if Allah willed" is taken as the object of "yaʾsa." It is also permissible that the complement of "yaʾsa" be omitted, indicated by the context; its estimate being: "from the faith of these people," and "that if Allah willed" would be in the genitive by an omitted lām of causation. The estimate: "because, if Allah willed, He would have guided mankind," so it would be a causal explanation for the denial of their absence of despair on the assumption of its occurrence.

"And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve, for what they have done, or to settle near their homes, until the promise of Allah comes. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise." It is conjoined upon the clause "And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion," in some respects of that clause. It is a threat of punishment for their obstinacy and persistence in not acknowledging the miracle of the Qur'an, and for their mockery in seeking to hasten the punishment with which they were threatened. So they were warned of what would befall them of fear through the arrival of raids and expeditions, which would strike those among whom they settle and frighten those around them, until the promise of Allah comes, on the day of Badr or the conquest of Makkah.

The use of "lā yazāl" in its original sense indicates reporting the continuation of an occurring matter. If this verse is Meccan, it must have been revealed at the time of some painful events befalling Quraysh, such as hunger or sickness. This verse would then be a warning to them that this is a punishment from Allah, and a threat that it will persist among them until the promise of Allah comes. Perhaps it was revealed during the period of their affliction by the seven years, indicated by His words: "And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives, and fruits" [al-Baqara: 155].

As for those who considered this surah Medinan, the interpretation of the verse according to them is that the calamity (al-qāriʿa) is a raiding expedition (sariyya) of the Muslims that goes out to threaten Quraysh and those around them. But there is no compulsion toward this.

Al-qāriʿa is originally a descriptive form from "al-qarʿ," which is striking one body against another. It is said: "qara'a al-bāb" when one strikes the door with a hand by its ring. Since striking produces a sudden noise that is alarming, because of that suddenness "al-qarʿ" became a metaphor for surprise and sudden onset, and similarly "al-ṭarq." They formed from this descriptive word a feminine form, indicating a modified noun that is necessarily omitted for brevity because of frequent use, which is interpreted as "the incident," "the occurrence," or "the calamity," as they say: "dāhiya" and "kārhtha," meaning a calamity described as alarming, since the sudden onset of misfortunes has a stronger effect on the soul. From this comes naming the hour of resurrection "al-qāriʿa."

What is meant here is a calamitous event, indicated by the attribution of striking to it. It is like a raid or a disaster that lands among them so that its punishment befalls them, or that occurs near them so that fear of its passing on to them afflicts them. Therefore "al-qāriʿa" does not mean raiding and fighting, since the name "al-qāriʿa" was not commonly applied to a battle. For this reason there is nothing in the verse indicating that it was revealed in Medina.

The meaning of "for what they have done" (bi-mā ṣanaʿū) is because of their deed, which is their disbelief and their ill treatment of their Prophet; and the relative pronoun was used because it is more comprehensive of their deeds.

The pronoun in "taḥul" refers to "qāriʿa," so it is a distribution of their state between being struck by calamities and calamities landing near their land, so they live in terror and dread of them.

It is also permissible that "taḥul" be an address to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: or you yourself, with the army, land near their homes. "Ḥulūl" means "alighting."

"Taḥul" is with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, the present tense of the intransitive "ḥalla." The ḍamma is obligatory for it, and this verb is among those that Buḥruq al-Yamani corrected Ibn Malik on in his commentary on verbs, and his correction is sound.

"Waʿd Allah" is an instance of the verbal noun used for the object, meaning "the promised thing of Allah," which is the punishment He threatened them with, as in His words: "Say to those who disbelieve: you will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and wretched is the resting place" [Ali 'Imran: 12]. The verse thus indicates their annihilation, since it mentions being overcome and entering Hell. So the meaning is that killing by the swords of the Muslims overcame them, which is the great onslaught. Among this is the day of Badr, the day of Hunayn, and the day of the Conquest.

"Ityan al-waʿd" (the coming of the promise) is a metaphor for its occurrence and its arrival.

The clause "Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise" is a concluding sentence (tadhyīl) for the clause "until the promise of Allah comes," signalling that the coming of the promise upon which the limit is set is certain, and that the limit by it is a limit tied to a matter near in occurrence. The emphasis is in consideration of the denial of the polytheists.

﴿And certainly were messengers ridiculed before you, so I gave respite to those who disbelieved; then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾ It is coordinated with the clause ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains were set in motion...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] and what follows it, because those three examples (mathal) mentioned there are things the polytheists asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for, in mockery and as a challenge, not because they were expected to occur.

It comes after the two clauses because of the relevance it has to them: in terms of the examples in the first, and in terms of the outcome (ghayah) in the second.

The people of Noah mocked him, peace be upon him: ﴿Every time a group of chiefs from his people passed by him, they ridiculed him﴾ [Hud: 38]. ʿAd mocked Hud, peace be upon him: ﴿So drop upon us pieces of the sky, if you are among the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 187]. Thamud mocked Salih, peace be upon him: ﴿The chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said, "Indeed, we see you in foolishness"﴾ [al-A'raf: 66]. They mocked Shu'ayb, peace be upon him: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we do with our wealth what we wish? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning"﴾ [Hud: 87]. Pharaoh mocked Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52].

Al-istihza' (mockery) is an intensified form of al-hazw (ridicule), like al-istiskhar in relation to al-sukhriyyah (derision).

Al-imla' (giving respite) means granting delay and leaving alone for a period. From it comes ﴿And forsake me for a long time﴾ [Maryam: 46]. It has already been discussed in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And those who denied Our signs, We will lead them gradually from where they do not know, and I will give them respite﴾ [al-A'raf: 182], in Surat al-A'raf.

The interrogative in ﴿so how was [My] punishment﴾ is for expressing wonder (al-ta'jib).

The word ʿiqab (punishment) originally was ʿiqabi (with the first-person suffix), like what was mentioned just before in His words ﴿and to Him is my return﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30]. The discourse is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, and a warning to the polytheists.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, commentary on Surah 13 (Ar-Ra'd), verse 33, part 1 of 2:

﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [as one with no partners]? Yet they assign partners to God. Say: "Name them. Or do you inform Him of something He does not know on earth, or [is it] mere outward speech?" Rather, their scheming has been made attractive to those who disbelieved, and they were turned away from the path. And whomever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾

The *fa'* (ف) that follows the interrogative *hamzah* (همزة الاستفهام, the interrogative particle "a") is postponed from its original position, because the interrogative *hamzah* has precedence (الصدارة, *al-sadarah*, the rule that interrogatives come first in their clause). The underlying structure of the wording is therefore: *afa-man huwa qa'im* ("so is He who is standing..."). Thus the *fa'* serves to make a consequence (تفريع, *tafri'*) of the interrogation, and it is not itself an interrogation that is consequent. This is the reason that the three conjunctions *wa*, *fa'* and *thumma* occur after the interrogative particle. This is the view of the verifiers (المحققين, *al-muhaqqiqin*, the careful scholars), in contrast to those who hold that the interrogation applies to the conjunction and what it conjoins.

So the *fa'* is a consequence of the statement ﴿Say: He is my Lord; there is no god but He. In Him I have put my trust﴾ [13:30], which answers their disbelief described in the phrase ﴿and they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾ [13:30]. The consequence in meaning is thus based on the two matters together: their disbelief, and the Prophet's ﷺ faith in God.

It is also possible that it is a consequence of the statement ﴿Even if a Qur'an by which mountains were moved [would not have believed]﴾ [13:31], in which case it is an escalation in the denial of their request for a miracle other than the Qur'an. That is: if you are amazed at their denial of the verses of the Qur'an, then more amazing than that is their making He who stands over every soul in what it has earned equal to those whom they have made partners with God.

It is also objected that, after this, their question about the mountains being moved, the earth being split, or the dead being made to speak is answered by reminding them of what befell the deniers before them, together with the consolation of the Messenger ﷺ, and this is why the denying interrogation is made a consequence.

The exegetes have various interpretations of the construction of the verse, many of them close to one another. The most sound of them returns to the view that there is an ellipsis in the wording, indicated by what is mentioned in it or indicated by the context. The correct way of explaining the wording is that the consequence is of the whole statement ﴿And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful; say: He is my Lord; there is no god but He﴾ [13:30]. That is, their disbelief in the Most Merciful and your belief that He is your Lord, to whom Lordship alone belongs, leads to a consequence: their interrogation, a denying interrogation directed at them, concerning their placing on equal footing He who stands over every soul with those whom they have made partners, who are not like Him. That is: how can they associate these with God when they are not equal to Him?

The referent of "He who stands over every soul" is God, the true God, the Creator, the Manager.

The predicate of "He who stands" is omitted, and it is indicated by the clause ﴿and they have assigned partners to God﴾. The sense is: "Is He who stands over every soul, and those whom they have made partners with Him, equal in deserving worship?" The implied predicate is indicated by what partnership in worship necessarily entails, namely equality in divinity and in deserving worship. The interrogation is a denial of that equality, which is understood from the word "partners" (شركاء). By means of this omitted element, there is no need to supply a counterpart (معادل, *mu'adil*) for the *hamzah*, as the author of *Mughni al-Labib* (مغني اللبيب, Ibn Hisham's grammar work) pointed out. This is because the implied element, indicated by a specific proof, is more useful than supplying a counterpart whose sense would be: "or is it one who is not like this?"

The later discussion of the phrase ﴿and they have assigned partners to God﴾ will come shortly.

The use of the relative pronoun (الموصول, *al-mawsul*) in place of the proper name of God in the phrase ﴿Is then He who stands﴾ is because the relative clause contains evidence of the absence of equality. It also rebukes the people of polytheism for making their gods partners of God in divinity, and it draws attention to their stupidity, since they themselves acknowledge that God is the Creator. The element assumed by their belief in this is the basis of establishing the proof against them through their own admission. It also contains an allusion to what will come shortly.

"He who stands over a thing" means its guardian, so the sense includes preservation, sustaining and provision. Because the word implies the meaning of "watcher" (الرقيب, *al-raqib*), it is followed by the preposition *'ala* ("over"), which indicates figurative elevation. Its root is from standing (القيام), which means constancy and continuance, as in His saying ﴿except while you are standing over him﴾ [3:75]. From the meaning of "standing" there also follows that He is the All-Knowing of the state of everything, because the completeness of self-subsistence (القيومية, *al-qayyumiyyah*) depends on the comprehensiveness of knowledge.

So the meaning of ﴿standing over every soul﴾ is: its administrator and manager in all its affairs, in creation, in its term, and in its provision, and the one who knows its states and deeds. Thus the use of the descriptive term "standing" here is an instance of using a shared term (المشترك, *al-mushtarak*) in both of its meanings. The polytheists do not dispute that God alone has this standing, but they do not take this into account in worshipping other than Him. For this reason the proof is binding upon them. To take this meaning into account, "standing" is connected to "over every soul" so that the standing extends to all its affairs.

The *bi-* (ب) in His saying ﴿in what it has earned﴾ indicates accompaniment (الملابسة, *al-mulabasah*). It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (حال, *hal*) either relating to "soul" or relating to "standing," according to what standing requires of knowledge. That is: a standing accompanied by what every soul has done, meaning a standing in accordance with its deeds: a deed of good requires standing over it with kindness and approval, and the effects of this appear in this world and in the Hereafter, according to His saying ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [16:97], and His saying ﴿God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth, as He granted it to those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and will surely substitute for them security after their fear﴾ [24:55]. Or it refers to a deed of evil, which requires standing over the soul with wrath and afflictions. In this relative clause, with its generality, there is thus both good tidings and warning for whoever among the two groups reflects. This is an allusion to both matters, directed at the two groups, conveyed by the relative clause.

The clause ﴿and they have assigned partners to God﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the *wa* (و) is that of circumstance, meaning: "while they have assigned partners to Him."

The appearance of the divine name (اسم الجلالة, *ism al-jalalah*, "God") in place of a pronoun referring back to "He who stands" is an appearance in the position where a pronoun would be expected. The purpose of this explicit naming is to express the named entity by its proper name, which is the original form, since the obligation of shifting away from it to the relative pronoun in the previous clause had already been fulfilled. The situation was thus ready for the proper name, and it makes clear that this is what is meant by the earlier relative pronoun, adding to the explicitness of the argument.

The clause ﴿Say: Name them﴾ is a resumptive statement (استئناف, *isti'naf*), with which the command to speak is repeated in order to attract attention and make the hearers mindful of what will be mentioned. This is a comprehensive expression, I mean the clause "name them," and it contains a refutation of them. The sense is: "Name them partners, for they have no share except the naming, that is, without the referent of the partner." The imperative is used in the sense of permission, as a metaphor (كناية, *kinayah*) for indifference to their calling them partners, like His saying ﴿Say: Be stones﴾ [17:50], and as you say to someone who makes a mistake in his speech: "Say whatever you like." The meaning is: these are only names that you have named, with no referents for them as divinities, because they are stones with no attributes of action. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You worship besides Him only names that you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority﴾ [12:40], and His saying ﴿They are only names that you have named﴾ [53:23]. This is a silencing of them and a mockery of their intellects, that they have deified what has no realities, so they have no excuse for this, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Or have they made for God partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed similar to them?﴾ [13:16]. The exegetes have strained greatly in interpreting ﴿Say: Name them﴾ with meanings that yield no real sense.

Then this is turned away from by the clause ﴿or do you inform Him of what He does not know on earth﴾. This is introduced by *am* (أم), the disjunctive *am* (المنقطعة, *al-munqati'ah*). The *am* indicates that what follows it has the sense of interrogation, which is a denying and rebuking interrogation: "It was not for you to invent lies against God and set up for Him partners about whose existence He has not informed you." Thus the phrase ﴿of what He does not know on earth﴾ is a metaphor for the non-existent, because what God does not know has no existence, for if it existed it would not be hidden from the knowledge of the All-Knowing of everything. The restriction of this to "on earth" intensifies their ignorance, for if anything were hidden from His knowledge, then what is unseen would be hidden from Him, and great existing things by your claim would not be hidden from Him.

In Surah Yunus, ﴿Say: Do you inform God of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?﴾ [10:18], there is an added generality.

The second *am* (أم) is connected (متصلة, *muttasilah*), serving as the counterpart (معادلة, *mu'adilah*) of the implied interrogative *hamzah* in ﴿or do you inform Him﴾, and the repetition of the *bi-* after *am* (the coordinating *am*) is for emphasis. The estimated sense is: "Rather, do you inform Him of what He does not know on earth? Rather, do you inform Him of mere outward speech?"

"Outward" (ظاهر, *zahir*) here is not from manifestness in the sense of clarity. Rather it derives from manifestness in the sense of departure, a metaphor for falsehood, meaning: by a mere saying that has no stability and is not true. Like the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*And that is a reproach, its shame departed from you*

and the saying of Sabra ibn 'Amr al-Faq'asi:

*You reproached us with their milk and their meat,*
*and that is a shame, O son of Rayta, that departs*

Here "that departs" (ظاهر) is used in the sense of disappearing and nullity.

His saying ﴿Rather, their scheming has been made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾ is a turning away from arguing against them by refuting the divinity of their idols, toward uncovering the cause. This is that the leaders of the polytheists made attractive to those who disbelieved their scheme against them, since it was by them that they were led to worship these idols.

"Scheming" (المكر, *al-makr*) is the concealment of means of harm. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers﴾ [3:54] at the beginning of Surah Al 'Imran, and at His saying ﴿Were they then secure from the scheme of God?﴾ [7:99] in Surah Al-A'raf, and at His saying ﴿And when those who disbelieved schemed against you﴾ [8:30] in Surah Al-Anfal. The intended meaning here is that the leaders of disbelief, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy, set up the worship of idols for the Arabs and made it appear good to them, showing them that it was truth and benefit, and they intended by this only to be leaders for them, so that they might dominate them and enslave them.

Since the passive verb requires an implied agent, His saying ﴿was made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾ is equivalent to your saying: "He made it attractive to them, something attractive." The thing made attractive, in the accusative form (مزيَّن), is what the discourse is about, namely the worship of idols. So the idols are semantically the object of the passive verb of making attractive. It is therefore determined that what follows this verb in the nominative is semantically the object, and accordingly "their scheme" is semantically the object. It is thus determined that "scheme" here means the worship of idols. On this basis, it is correct that the genitive "their" (referring to the disbelievers) in "scheme of them" is a genitive of the verbal noun governing what is semantically an object, namely the object marked by the transitive *bi-*. That is: "the scheme against them by those who made it attractive to them."

This argument contains several features and particularities:

First: a rebuke of them for analogizing their idols with God in establishing divinity for them, an analogy that is invalid because there is no common ground. How then can He who stands over every soul be equated with those who have none of this?

Second: a rebuke of them for making names that have no referents into gods.

Third: a refutation of their idols being gods by the fact that they know nothing as gods. This is a metaphor for the negation of their divinity.

Fourth: that their claim of gods is merely speech that does not correspond to reality, and this is His saying ﴿or is it mere outward speech?﴾.

Fifth: that this is a false embellishment that the propagandists of disbelief promoted among them, and this is the meaning of calling it a scheme in His saying ﴿Rather, their scheming has been made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾.

Sixth: that they bar people from the path of guidance.

The coordination of "and they were turned away from the path" with the clause ﴿their scheming has been made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾ is made in the sense that the content of both clauses concerns the state of the polytheists. The first clause concerns them as objects, and the second concerns them as subjects of the turning away, after they had been affected by disbelief. The majority of readers read it with *fath* on the *sad* (صُدُّوا as "they were turned away" read as *Ṣaddū*, with a fatha on the ṣād). The reading of 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf is with a *damma* on the *sad* (صُدُّوا, *ṣuddū*), so that the content of both clauses is that "those who disbelieved" is the object of the making attractive and of the turning away.

The clause ﴿And whomever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ is a concluding summary (تذييل, *tadhyil*) for what it contains of generality.

﴿The parable of the Garden that the God-fearing have been promised: beneath it rivers flow; its food is everlasting, and so is its shade. *Al-mathal* (the parable, or striking description) here means the remarkable attribute. It was said that this is a true (literal) meaning of *al-mathal*, as in His saying: ﴿To God belongs the highest description﴾ [16:60]. It was also said that it is a metaphorical extension from *al-mathal* in its sense of a likeness in a remarkable condition, applied to a remarkable condition that is not a likeness, because it deserves to be compared to it.

The clause ﴿beneath it rivers flow﴾ is a predicate of *mathal*, taken as a predicate about what belongs to the annexed noun (*al-mudaf ilayhi*). It describes the annexed noun because of the strong connection between the two terms of the annexation, as one says: "the description of Zayd is that he is dark-complexioned."

The clause ﴿its food is everlasting﴾ is a second predicate. *Al-ukul* (with a *damma* on the *alif*) means what is eaten, and this was discussed earlier.

The permanence of the shade is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the interlacing of the trees, such that there is no gap between them through which the sun can pass, as He said: ﴿and gardens thickly planted﴾ [78:16]. This is among the praiseworthy qualities and pleasures of the Gardens.

The clause ﴿That is the final outcome of those who guarded themselves against God﴾ is a new sentence (*mustanfa'a*).

The meaning is: that is the one you heard to be the final outcome of the abode for those who fulfil the covenant of God, up to His saying: ﴿and they avert evil with good﴾ [13:22], up to His saying: ﴿How excellent is the final outcome of the abode﴾ [13:24]. The clause ﴿and the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾ is a new sentence, connected by contrast (*al-munasabah bi al-mudadda*). It serves as an explanation of His saying: ﴿and theirs is the evil abode﴾ [13:25].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 37:

﴿And thus We have sent it down as a judgment, in Arabic. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have no protector from Allah, nor any defender.﴾ It is an interjection (i'tiraD) and a conjunction ( 'atf) upon the clause ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book rejoice in what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 36]. When he mentioned the condition of the People of the Two Books in receiving the Qur'an at its revelation, he turned to the condition of the Arabs in this matter, by way of allusion (ta'ridh), censuring the poor reception given to it by its polytheist (mushrik) people, although they were the most deserving of all people to receive it well, since it was revealed in their tongue, containing what is good for them and what enlightens their minds. The chief purpose of this was made to be the exaltation of the Qur'an's lofty status in both wording and meaning, and within this is embedded an allusion to the polytheists among the Arabs.

As to the demonstrative in His words ﴿and thus﴾, the discussion is like that which preceded in His words ﴿Thus have We sent you to a community﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30].

The pronoun of the absent in ﴿We have sent it down﴾ refers to what was sent down to you in His words ﴿rejoice in what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 36].

The prepositional phrase formed by the demonstrative functions as a substitute for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). The estimate is: We have sent it down a sending like that sending.

﴿A judgment, Arabic﴾ are two circumstantial accusatives (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿We have sent it down﴾. Here, ḥukm (judgment) carries the meaning of ḥikmah (wisdom), as in His words ﴿And We gave him judgment while a child﴾ [Maryam: 12]. The very essence of judgment was made a circumstance of it for the sake of emphasis. The meaning is that it possesses judgment, that is, wisdom. Wisdom has already been discussed.

﴿Arabic﴾ is a second circumstantial accusative, and is not an adjective of ﴿judgment﴾, since wisdom is not described by reference to nations; rather the meaning is that it is wisdom expressed in the Arabic language. The intended sense is that it is in the language of the Arabs, which is the most eloquent, most beautiful and easiest of languages, and in this lies its inimitability (i'jaz). Thus this Book attains two perfections: a perfection in terms of its meanings and aims, which is that it is judgment, and a perfection in terms of its wording, which is alluded to by its being Arabic. This is something no Book before it attained, because wisdom is the most noble of intelligibles, so it is fitting that its conveyance be in the noblest language and the most apt for expressing wisdom. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 192] ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193] ﴿upon your heart, that you may be among the warners﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 194] ﴿in clear Arabic speech﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 195].

Then, in its being Arabic there is a favour upon the Arabs addressed by it first, in that it is in their language, and that in this lies the goodness of their repute; so there is in it an allusion to the poor judgment of the disbelievers among them, since they did not give thanks for this blessing, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿We have indeed sent down to you a Book in which is your mention. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10]. Malik said: In it is the preservation of your remembrance.

The clause ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ is parenthetical, and the lam is introductory to an oath (lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam). The plural pronoun in His words ﴿their desires﴾ refers to something known from the context, namely the polytheists to whom the address is directed.

Following their desires may imply striving to fulfil their request for a sign other than the Qur'an, with a warning that God might grant their request for what they asked, as He said to Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ [Hud: 46].

The meaning of ﴿the knowledge that has come to you﴾ is what reached you and what you were taught. It is possible that by the relative clause is meant the Qur'an, as an honouring of it; that is: if you were to side with them and ask us for a sign other than the Qur'an after the Qur'an has been revealed to you, or after We have informed you that We will not descend to fulfil their proposals. It is also possible that following their religion is meant, since their religion is desires, and the referent of ﴿the knowledge that has come to you﴾ would then be the religion of Islam.
The walī is the helper, and the wāqī is the defender.

The negation of a helper and a supporter has been made the answer to the condition, as a metonymy for the answer, which is retribution and punishment.

The aim of this is to warn the Muslims against inclining toward the deceptions of the polytheists, and to warn against returning to their religion, stirring up their steadfastness in their religion, following His words, exalted is He: ﴿It has been revealed to you and to those before you: If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and to despair the polytheists of hoping that a sign will come that accords with their proposals.

The ﴿min﴾ that enters upon the divine name is connected to ﴿walī﴾ and ﴿wāqī﴾, and the ﴿min﴾ that enters upon ﴿walī﴾ serves to emphasise the negation, as an explicit statement of generality. The disagreement between the majority of scholars and Ibn Kathir has already been discussed concerning their deletion of the yā' of wāqin in both pausal and continuous recitation, and Ibn Kathir's retention of the yā' in pausal position but not in continuous recitation, in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7] in this surah.

And We had already sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring. It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah.

This returns to refuting the polytheists, who denied the sign of the Qur'an and insisted on demanding a sign of their own choosing, one like the signs given to Musa and 'Isa, peace be upon them both. The verse shows that the Messenger brings no signs except by the permission of Allah, and that this does not depend on the proposals of peoples. This is His saying: ﴿It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah.﴾ The sentence is therefore joined by conjunction to the sentence ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 37].

Woven into this refutation is the removal of a doubt that may occur, or has occurred, to some polytheists, who criticised or did criticise the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the ground that he marries women, and that it is the nature of a prophet not to concern himself with women. Al-Baghawi said: "It is narrated that the Jews, and it is said that the polytheists, said: 'This man has no aspiration except for women.'" If the report concerning the occasion of revelation is sound, it is certain that those who said this were the polytheists, since this sura is Meccan, and the Jews had no dealings with the people of Makkah, nor was there any of them in Makkah. It does not follow that this verse was revealed on a specific occasion. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married Khadijah and then Sawdah, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in Makkah. It is therefore possible that the polytheists made this statement as a denial, clinging to the weakest of the grounds for attacking prophethood. This is a doubt that occurs to the naive or to those who deceive, and the missionaries among the Christians may use it to deceive the weak in faith, preferring 'Isa (peace be upon him) over Muhammad (ﷺ) on the basis that 'Isa did not marry women. This does not succeed with the wise, because that is one of the permissible portions of worldly enjoyment and does not entail superiority. Superiority in every work is measured only by the degree of perfections contained in that work. No one knows the wisdom for which 'Isa (peace be upon him) did not marry a woman. Yahya (peace be upon him) was a chaste man (ḥaṣūr), so it may be that 'Isa (peace be upon him) was like him, because Allah does not burden him with what is hard for him, or with what He did not burden any other of the prophets and messengers with. As for Allah's description of Yahya (peace be upon him) with His saying "and chaste" [Āl 'Imrān: 39], it is not meant to be a virtue in itself. Rather, He informed his father Zakariyya (peace be upon him) that he would have no offspring, so that he would know that Allah had answered his supplication and granted him Yahya (peace be upon him) as an honour from Him. Then He decreed that he would have no offspring, to carry out His decree, and made his wife barren. The explanation of this has already been given in the tafsir (exegesis) of Surat Āl 'Imrān. Most of the messengers had wives, and most of them had offspring, such as Nuh, Ibrahim, Lut, Musa, Dawud, Sulayman, and others besides these, peace be upon them all.

"Azwāj" is the plural of "zawj," and this is an instance of pairing plural with plural. Some messengers had only one wife, such as Nuh and Lut, peace be upon them both, and others had several wives, such as Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them all.

Since the aim of the refutation is to show that taking a wife does not conflict with the attribute of messengership, there was no need to enumerate the many wives of some of them.

The discussion of the word "zawj" has already occurred at His saying, "And We said: O Adam, dwell you and your spouse in the Garden" [al-Baqarah: 35], in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Dhurriyyah" means offspring. It has already been discussed at His saying, "He said: And of my offspring" [al-Baqarah: 124], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence ﴿It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah﴾ is the main point, and it is joined to the sentence ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you﴾. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 13, verse 40:

﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We cause you to die, your duty is only to convey (the message), and upon Us is the reckoning﴾. It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39], in view of what it conveys of the ambiguity of Allah's intent regarding the terms of the threat and the times of the revelation of the verses. So this sentence clarifies that the Prophet (ﷺ) is not commanded to occupy himself with that, nor to await it; rather he is a conveyor from Allah to His servants, and Allah knows what He will call His servants to account for, whether the Prophet (ﷺ) witnesses that or does not witness it.

He made tawaffi (causing to die) a metonymy for not seeing the threat fall upon them, by the indication of its being contrasted with His saying "We show you." The meaning: your duty is only to convey, whether you see their punishment or do not see it.

In the use of the word (some) (ba'd) there is an indication that he sees some of it. In this there is a warning to them that the threat will descend upon them even if it is delayed; and that this religion continues after the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). For if the threat which he was commanded to convey is realized even after his death, then it is more fitting that his law, for the sake of which it came, and the threat against the disbelievers in it, should be a law that continues after him, since the means cannot be of greater importance than the end for which it is intended.

The emphasis of the condition with the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) and the added (ma) after the conditional (in) is intended to emphasize the connection between this condition and its answer, which is ﴿your duty is only to convey, and upon Us is the reckoning﴾. Moreover, the energetic nun is not attached to the conditional verb except when (ma) is added after (in), so the intention of emphasis necessitates bringing two emphasizers, and this is only for the purpose of a strong emphasis.

He did not show him some of it, such as the punishment of the people of apostasy (ridda), for most of them were deniers who concealed disbelief, like Musaylima the Liar.

In the verse there is an indication that the punishment which befalls those who deny His Messenger (ﷺ) is confined to the deniers and does not strike anyone other than the denier, because it is extermination by the sword, which is divisible; and the variation of times is a mercy from Allah to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The (ʿalā) in His saying ﴿upon you is the conveyance and upon Us is the reckoning﴾ is used in the sense of obligation and binding; it is literal in the first and metaphorical in the second, meaning that it is obligatory upon Allah by His own commitment to it.

The (innama) is restrictive (li'l-hasr), and what is restricted is the conveyance, because it is the element delayed in mention within the clause that follows the restrictive particle. The sense is: upon you is only the conveyance and not anything else, such as the sending down of signs or the hastening of punishment. For this reason he placed the predicate before the subject to specify what is restricted.

The clause ﴿and upon Us is the reckoning﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿upon you is the conveyance﴾, so it is, in meaning, governed by the restrictive particle. The sense is: "and only upon Us is the reckoning," i.e., calling them to account for denial, not the reckoning of granting their proposals.

[Page 171]

The verse is coordinated (*'ataf*) with the clause ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾ [Yunus: 46], which is linked to the clause ﴿For every term is a Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38]. It follows this clause to warn the deniers that the signs of the Prophet's ﷺ victory have appeared and its first dawn has broken, so that they may reflect on their own situation. The sentence that follows the coordinated clause comes as a safeguard, lest they suppose that the punishment is slow and will not befall them. It is also good news to the Prophet ﷺ that God will manifest his victory during his lifetime, since its signs have already come. It is therefore also a safeguard, lest the Prophet ﷺ despair of seeing his victory, even though he knows that God will perfect His light through this religion.

The interrogative in ﴿أوَلَمْ يَرَوْا﴾ is rhetorical denial (*inkari*), and the pronoun refers to the deniers, the same referent as the pronoun in (*na'iduhum*, "We promise them"). The statement is a threat, intended to rouse them to what has crept upon them of the phantoms of decline through the diminishing of the land, that is, of its inhabitants.

The seeing (*ru'ya*) may be visual, meaning the traces of that diminishment are seen. It may also be cognitive, meaning: have they not known what befell the lands of the earlier nations of diminishment?

The definiteness of "the land" (*al-ard*) is generic (*ta'rif al-jins*), meaning We come to any land of the nations. The word "land" is used here figuratively (*majaz*) for its people, as in God's words ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. The indication is that the verb of diminishing is attached to it, since diminishment does not occur in the substance of the land itself, nor is any reduction seen in it, but it befalls those who dwell upon it. This is the same as God's words ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen what was the end of those before them? God destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are the like of them﴾ [Muhammad: 10].

Many exegetes (*mufassirun*) held that the land refers to the land of the disbelievers of Quraysh. In this case the definiteness is for a specific reference (*al-'ahd*), the seeing is visual, and the verse is a rousing for them, as when Muslims overcame the land of the enemy and it passed out of its control. Thus the land under their management diminishes, while the land subject to the people of Islam grows. On this basis they held that this verse was revealed in Madinah, and this is what led some to say that Surat al-Ra'd is Madinan. If it is considered Madinan, then the "edges" (*atraf*) may be explained as two edges, namely Makkah and Madinah, for they are the two edges of the lands of the Arabs. The edge of Makkah on the side of Yemen, and the edge of Madinah on the side of the Levant (al-Sham). The number of disbelievers in both towns continued to decline through the conversion of their disbelievers, until Madinah became purely Muslim, and then Makkah became so after the Day of the Conquest.

Whatever the interpretation of the verse, the cause of its revelation, and its place of revelation, the verse is a warning that they are heading to annihilation and that they are defeated and will vanish, like His words in another verse, in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, diminishing it from its edges? Are they the victors?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44], meaning: they are not the victors. This is a respite for them and a sufficient warning, perhaps they will amend their affairs.

The clause ﴿God judges; there is no repeller of His judgment﴾ is coordinated (*'ataf*) with the clause ﴿Have they not seen﴾, and confirms the purpose of it, which is the argument that the delay of the threat does not indicate its falsity. He therefore argued for this with the clause ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾ [Yunus: 46], then with the clause ﴿Have they not seen that We come to the land﴾, then with the clause ﴿God judges﴾. The meaning is that whatever punishment God has decreed cannot be annulled by anyone, that it will certainly occur even if it is delayed.

For this reason the clause ﴿there is no repeller of His judgment﴾ occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and it is the one that qualifies the intended verb, since it is the focus of the speech. The aim is not to inform that God judges, for that is hardly hidden, but the aim is to alert to the fact that there is no repeller of His judgment. The negation of the genus of "repeller" (*mu'aqqib*) conveys the absence of everything that could be a repeller, whether a partner, an intercessor, one who calls upon Him, one who desires, one who seeks protection, or one who ransoms.

The *mu'aqqib* is one who undoes an action and nullifies it. It is derived from *'aqib* (heel, that which comes after), and this is a metaphor (*isti'ara*) that became so common that it became a literal usage. It was mentioned earlier at God's words ﴿For him are repellers (*mu'aqqibat*)﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11] in this surah, as if it comes after the one who did the deed.

The explicit mention of the Name of Majesty (Allah) after the pronoun in ﴿that We come to the land﴾ serves to cultivate awe, and to remind of what the great Name contains of the meaning of divinity and oneness, which requires that there be no contender. It also makes the clause self-standing, since it is like a maxim (*hikma*) and a proverb (*mathal*).

The clause ﴿and He is swift in reckoning﴾ may be coordinated with the clause ﴿God judges﴾, so that it becomes a fourth proof that His promise will certainly come to pass, and that its delay, however long, is nothing but swift in terms of the certainty of its occurrence. It may also be coordinated with the circumstantial clause. The meaning is: He judges with a judgment that is not diminished, and His reckoning is swift. The outcome of both interpretations is the same.

*Al-hisab* (reckoning) is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for requital.

*Al-sur'a* (swiftness) is haste, and it is in everything according to its nature.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 13, verse 42:**

﴿Indeed, those before them plotted, but to Allah belongs all plotting. He knows what every soul earns, and the disbelievers will know to whom the final home belongs.﴾

Since His saying ﴿Do they not see that We come upon the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41] was a threat and a warning, like His saying ﴿So its portents have already come﴾ [Muhammad: 18], and it is a warning with a threat against their pretense of asking for signs while they conceal their determination to deny and to persist in denial, their actions were described as plotting (makr), and they were compared with the earlier deniers, as in His saying ﴿No town that We destroyed believed before them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 6]. In this comparison there is an allusion (ramz) that their end is like the end of the nations they knew. So the reduction of this people's land from its outskirts is, from Allah's plotting against them, a recompense for their plotting. For this reason it is followed by His saying ﴿Indeed, those before them plotted﴾, meaning: just as these people plotted.

The clause ﴿Indeed, those before them plotted﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah).

The clause ﴿but to Allah belongs all plotting﴾ is a consequence (tafri') of the clause ﴿Do they not see that We come upon the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41], and of the clause ﴿Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41].

The meaning is: these people plotted, and those before them plotted, and punishment befell those before them. So Allah plotted against them, and He plots against these people with a great plot, just as He plotted against those before them.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿but to Allah belongs all plotting﴾ serves exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning: it belongs to Him and not to anyone else, because His plotting cannot be repelled by any repeller. The plotting of others is then like no plotting at all, as evidenced by the fact that He attributed plotting to them in His saying ﴿Indeed, those before them plotted﴾. This has the same meaning as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah is the best of the plotters﴾ [al-Anfal: 30].

He emphasized the implication of exclusivity by His saying (jami'an, "all"), which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "plotting". This was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾ [Yunus: 4] in Surah Yunus.

The whole of plotting was attributed to Allah only by treating the plotting of others as if it did not exist. Therefore the restriction (qasr) in His saying ﴿but to Allah belongs all plotting﴾ is claimed (idda'i), and the generality in His saying (jami'an) is an ascribed generality (tanzili).

The clause ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾ stands in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿but to Allah belongs all plotting﴾. Since He knows what every soul earns, whether its outward or inward earning, His plotting is stronger than the plotting of any soul, for nothing that souls conceal of plotting escapes Him. Otherwise some of their plotting would go unanswered by anything stronger. The mighty and powerful One who knows the unseen may have a severer punishment, while a weak person may surpass others through cunning.

The clause ﴿and the disbelievers will know to whom the final home belongs﴾ is coordinated (atf) with the clause ﴿but to Allah belongs all plotting﴾. By "the disbeliever" is meant the category (jins), that is, the disbelievers. The phrase "the final home" (uqba al-dar) was mentioned just before, meaning: they will know that the final home belongs to the believers and not to the disbelievers. So the statement is an allusive threat (ta'rid bi'l-wa'id).

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿the disbeliever (al-kafir)﴾ in the singular. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿the disbelievers (al-kuffar)﴾ in the plural. The singular and plural are equivalent when the noun is defined by the generic article (al-jins).

[Page 174]

[Page 175]

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book."﴾ This is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical conjunction) with what is implied by the clause ﴿And those before them had already plotted﴾ [al-Ra'd: 42], in the sense of allusion, namely that their saying ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27] was a form of scheming, by displaying that they were seeking the signs that indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), while pretending that they were in doubt. They had, from time to time, disclosed what they concealed, and so they spoke plain denial and went beyond the stage of scheming to the stage of openly declaring disbelief, saying: ﴿You are not a messenger.﴾

Their saying has been related in the present tense (*mudari'*) to indicate its repetition on their part, and to bring to mind their strange condition of persisting in denial after they had seen the proofs of truthfulness. In the same way, the present tense is used in His saying ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾ [Hud: 38] and His saying ﴿He argues with Us concerning the people of Lut﴾ [Hud: 74]. Since their statement related here is plain, with no ambiguity in it, the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to give a reply that admits no dispute, namely that Allah judge between him and them.

The Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to answer them as one confident of his truthfulness, calling upon as testimony to that the testimony of truthfulness, namely the calling to witness of Allah the Exalted and the calling to witness of those who know the earlier Scriptures and laws.

Since testimony to the Messenger's (ﷺ) truthfulness is a testimony against those who disbelieved, that they are liars, the testimony was made to be between him and them.

The calling of Allah as witness carries the sense of swearing an oath to the truth, like the saying of Hud (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, I call Allah to witness﴾ [Hud: 54].

The preposition *ba'* (bi-) attached to the Name of Majesty, which is the agent (*fa'il*) of *kafa* (suffices), is for emphasis.

[Page 176]

The original structure is: "Allah suffices," and *shahidan* (as a witness) is a necessary circumstantial accusative (*hal lazima*) or a specification (*tamyiz*). That is: Allah suffices in respect of being the witness.

﴿And whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ is coordinated with the Name of Majesty.

The relative pronoun in ﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ may be taken to mean the category of whoever is characterised by the relative clause. The meaning is: "and everyone among them who has knowledge of the Book." The singular form of the pronoun attached to *'inda* (with) is in consideration of the wording of *man* (whoever). The definiteness of "the Book" is definiteness by prior reference (*'ahd*), and it refers to the Torah. That is: and the testimony of the scholars of the Book. This is because the Jews, before the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration to Madinah, used to seek support against the polytheists by the coming of a prophet confirming the Torah.

It is also possible that what is meant by "whoever has knowledge of the Book" is a specific person, namely Waraqah ibn Nawfal, when the people of Makkah knew that he testified that what had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the *Namus* (the divine law-bearer, i.e. the angel of revelation) that had been sent down to Musa (peace be upon him), as in the report of the beginning of revelation (*bad' al-wahy*) in the Sahih. Waraqah was alone in knowledge of the Torah and the Gospel. The report of his saying to the Prophet (ﷺ) what he said was well known among the Quraysh.

Thus the definiteness in "the Book" is the definiteness of the genus (*jins*) restricted to the Torah and the Gospel.

It has also been said that what is meant is 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) at the start of his arrival in Madinah. But this is far-fetched, since the surah is Meccan, as has passed. The basis of the testimony of the scholars of the Book to the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) is their finding the good tidings of a prophet, the seal of the messengers (ﷺ), and their finding that what came in the Qur'an agrees with the patterns of the divine laws and explains the symbols found in the Torah and the Gospel concerning the description of the promised, confirmed Prophet (ﷺ). For this meaning, the expression in this verse is "whoever has knowledge of the Book" rather than "the People of the Book," because the application of this is not perceived except by their scholars. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 197].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Ibrahim

This surah has been attributed to the name of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), so that this became its name, and no other name is known for it. I have not come across the use of this name for it in the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ) or in the speech of his Companions in any reliable report.

The reason for naming it thus, although the mention of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) occurs in many surahs, is that it is among the surahs beginning with *Alif Lam Ra*. Some of them have been distinguished from one another by attribution to the names of prophets (peace be upon them) whose stories occur in them, or to the place of the mission of some of them, as in Surah al-Hijr. For this reason, Surah al-Ra'd was not attributed to anything of this kind, because it is distinguished by its opening, with the addition of the letter *mim* to *alif, lam* and *ra*.

It is entirely Meccan according to the majority. It is related from Qatadah that except for two verses, ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favour of Allah for disbelief?﴾ [Ibrahim: 28] up to His saying ﴿and wretched is the settlement﴾ [Ibrahim: 29]. It has also been said: up to His saying ﴿Indeed, your destination is the Fire﴾ [Ibrahim: 30]. This was revealed concerning the polytheists in the matter of Badr, but that is only a supposition, as you will know.

These surahs were revealed after Surah al-Shura and before Surah al-Anbiya'. It is counted as the seventieth in the order of the surahs by revelation.

Its verses are counted as fifty-four according to the Madinans, fifty according to the people of Syria, fifty-one according to the people of Basra, and fifty-two according to the people of Kufa.

* * *

[Page 178]

Among its themes: it begins by drawing attention to the inimitability of the Qur'an, and by exalting its status, and that it was sent down to bring people out of misguidance, and by the favour of making it in the tongue of the Arabs; and by glorifying Allah the Exalted who sent it down; and by warning those who disbelieve in it, by the one to whom it was sent down.

It also awakens the obstinate to the fact that Muhammad (ﷺ) was not an innovator among the messengers, and that his being a human being is not something incompatible with his mission from Allah, like the others among the messengers. He gives him the example of the mission of Musa (peace be upon him) to Pharaoh, for the reform of the condition of the Children of Israel; and by reminding his people of the blessings of Allah and the obligation to be grateful for them; and by admonishing them with what befell the people of Nuh, 'Ad, and those after them, and what their messengers met with of denial, and how the end of the deniers was; and by establishing the proof of the oneness of Allah the Exalted in divinity through the evidence of His creatures; and by mentioning the Resurrection; and by warning the disbelievers against being deceived by their leaders and great ones, through the scheming of Satan; and how they will disown them on the Day of Gathering; and by describing their condition and the condition of the believers on that day.

And the excellence of the word of Islam and the wickedness of the word of disbelief.

Then, the marvelling at the condition of a people who disbelieved the favour of Allah and caused those who followed them to enter the abode of ruin through association.

And an allusion to its contrast with the condition of the believers.

And the enumeration of some of His blessings upon people in detail, then their gathering in summary.

[Page 179]

Then He reminded both groups of the condition of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), so that both groups might know who follows the path of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and who turns away from it among the inhabitants of the Sacred Land; and by warning them against denying the blessing; and by warning them that what befell those who wronged before them may befall them.

And by strengthening the Prophet (ﷺ) with the promise of victory, and what intervened of parables in that; and it is concluded with comprehensive words from His saying ﴿This is a message for the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 52] to its end.
